A Delray Beach man says the city denied his mother a burial plot at the municipal cemetery where generations of his family are laid to rest — and he says the problem is about far more than space.Kevin Mitchell, who was born and raised in Delray Beach, said his mother died in June. When he sought to have her buried at Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery, where her parents, grandmother and two of her children are already interred, he was told there was no room.WATCH: Delray Beach cemetery concerns grow as man says mother was denied burial plot"My mother spent her career as a school teacher over 32 years," Mitchell said. "Two of her kids are buried here, her parents are buried over there on the far south side. Her grandmother is buried over here to my left. And she's not here."Mitchell said the problem became clear months before his mother died, when she was in hospice. He said the city told him he would have to wait until after her passing to reserve a plot. When she died in June, he was told the cemetery was at capacity — leaving her buried in Broward County.A cemetery at the center of the community's historyMitchell said the cemetery holds deep significance for many people, particularly Delray Beach's Black community, and that its deteriorating condition is an affront to the people buried there."This cemetery encompasses so many of these residents including myself, our lives, our parents, our loved ones, the legacy and the history of this community," Mitchell said.This is not the first time concerns have been raised about the cemetery. Previous reporting revealed that a software error led to pre-purchased plots being sold to other people. Residents have also raised concerns about weeds, sinking ground and toppled grave markers."You can't read the names anymore, their names are no longer legible," Mitchell said.'A lot should've been done'Mitchell said the problems have been building for years and that he is frustrated by the lack of action."I feel very hurt. I feel that a lot should've been done, a lot could've been done and there were mishaps, and missteps that need to be corrected," Mitchell said.His concerns deepened recently when he observed approximately nine graves being dug over a weekend, leading him to question whether space truly is as limited as the city has indicated."As you can see, those were the graves that were dug and now they're covered up," Mitchell said.City points to mausoleum constructionThe city is pointing to the construction of a $2,875,010 mausoleum as a solution, which would add more than 2,000 spaces to the cemetery.Mitchell acknowledged the project but said it does not address the needs of everyone."It will be beautiful once it's completed, it's excellent. But until you have some residents that do not wish to be entombed, they wish to be interred," Mitchell said. "It's a solution but it's a bandaid to the overall problem."State lawmaker calls preservation a priorityState Rep. Rob Long, a former Delray Beach vice mayor, said the issues at the cemetery are serious and that preserving its history must be a priority."The issues at Delray Beach Memorial Gardens are serious, and preserving a cemetery that holds so much of Delray's history has to be a priority," Long said in a statement. "The State has already invested in documenting and preserving the site through the historic resource survey, and as the City works through what additional capital and preservation needs remain, I want to be at the table to help identify solutions and determine where the state may be able to assist through grants, appropriations, or other resources."Historic survey findings and what comes nextThe city commissioned LG2 Environmental Solutions to conduct a historic resource survey of the original section of the cemetery, funded through a State of Florida Small Matching Grant. The survey documented more than 1,200 historic graves, found that 94% of markers are in fair to poor condition, and recommended the site as potentially eligible for listing on the National Register of Historic Places.The report called for expanded fieldwork, improved landscaping practices, professional repairs and enhanced public outreach.The city said it expects to select a consultant this week to review operations and recommend improvements.Mitchell said he will keep pushing for accountability — including his call for a permanent on-site office at the cemetery."I will advocate until the sun goes down and the sun comes up that they put an office on site right here at the cemetery," Mitchell said.He said the fight is personal."It grieves me greatly to even have to deal with this and fight this fight, but I'm fighting it for my mother who is deceased," Mitchell said. "We as citizens need to make sure we're doing all that we can to make sure that they're being respected and that their wishes are being honored."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie County could become a data center, according to a rezoning application sent to the city of Fort Pierce.Willow Lakes LLC, the owner of 203 acres of land off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, submitted a rezoning application in June to change 174 acres to light industrial use to allow for a data center.WATCH BELOW: New 203-acre data center proposed in St. Lucie CountyThe rezoning application said, "the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial."Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area."You have a beautiful view all the time," Whiteside said.When asked about the potential data center, her reaction was immediate."I hate that idea," Whiteside said.The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project."He was looking at what else he could potentially do at the property," Dobbins said.Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system.According to the rezoning application, the applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, "intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and/or restaurants/fast food."Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions."Data centers are kind of the rage right now," Broderick said.Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution."If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said.The rezoning application said that if rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. According to the application, "the partner company would need to submit to the City a site plan application for the proposed data center and obtain City approval of the site plan."The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board on Sept.

On one hand, we have a technology that has proven to be an important tool for our officers and investigators and has helped us protect people and solve crimes, he said. On the other, we have a responsibility to listen to our community, respect the direction of our state leaders, and ensure our policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety. A packed crowd filled Village Hall Tuesday night as residents urged leaders to hit the pause button on future hyperscale data center projects . But by the end of the meeting, the debate over data centers had led to a major shakeup in village leadership. After hours of public comment, the Indiantown Village Council voted 4-1 against a proposed resolution that would have temporarily paused new large-scale data center applications while the village drafted regulations addressing infrastructure, utilities and community impacts. Council members said they want new legal counsel to review the proposal and help craft language that can withstand legal scrutiny before bringing it back for consideration. Shortly after that vote, the council voted to terminate Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had served the village since 2024, effective immediately. The council also voted to remove Village Attorney Wade Vose from the meeting and move forward with obtaining interim legal counsel. Vose had previously submitted his resignation, but council members voted to end his participation in the meeting and proceed in a different direction. Late Tuesday night, the council appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager. Giardino recently served as Stuart's city manager before being fired by the Stuart City Commission last week. Council members said the leadership changes reflect a desire to move the village in a new direction as it tackles major issues, including future data center development. As she left Village Hall, Kryzda offered a brief response to CBS12 News. "I'm happy to go home early." Before the vote, residents spent hours voicing concerns about the potential impact multiple hyperscale data centers could have on the community. Some residents created a website featuring an interactive map highlighting several proposed projects across the area. Penny Kaminsky-Preli used the map to point out some of those developments. "This is Project Growler, another 600,000 hyperscale data center. Another one in the application." Others worried about how close future projects could be to schools, parks and neighborhoods. "I'm not against them coming to the village. I'm more concerned with their proximity to things like the school or field elementary school. I'm more concerned with the proximity to Booker Park," resident Eric Miller said. Former Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback urged council members to use what he described as authority recently granted to local governments by state lawmakers. "There have been 19 moratoriums that have been passed in Florida this year. Not a single one of them have been challenged by a data center plaintiff," Fishback said. Village leaders told CBS12 News they expect to have interim legal counsel in place soon and hope to bring a revised data center resolution back before the council within the next week or two.

A Delray Beach man says the city denied his mother a burial plot at the municipal cemetery where generations of his family are laid to rest — and he says the problem is about far more than space.Kevin Mitchell, who was born and raised in Delray Beach, said his mother died in June. When he sought to have her buried at Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery, where her parents, grandmother and two of her children are already interred, he was told there was no room.WATCH: Delray Beach cemetery concerns grow as man says mother was denied burial plot"My mother spent her career as a school teacher over 32 years," Mitchell said. "Two of her kids are buried here, her parents are buried over there on the far south side. Her grandmother is buried over here to my left. And she's not here."Mitchell said the problem became clear months before his mother died, when she was in hospice. He said the city told him he would have to wait until after her passing. When she died in June, he was told the cemetery was at capacity — leaving her buried in Broward County.A cemetery at the center of the community's historyMitchell said the cemetery holds deep significance for many people, particularly Delray Beach's Black community, and that its deteriorating condition is an affront to the people buried there."This cemetery encompasses so many of these residents including myself, our lives, our parents, our loved ones, the legacy and the history of this community," Mitchell said.This is not the first time concerns have been raised about the cemetery. Previous reporting revealed that a software error led to pre-purchased plots being sold to other people. Residents have also raised concerns about weeds, sinking ground and toppled grave markers."You can't read the names anymore, their names are no longer legible," Mitchell said.'A lot should've been done'Mitchell said the problems have been building for years and that he is frustrated by the lack of action."I feel very hurt. I feel that a lot should've been done, a lot could've been done and there were mishaps, and missteps that need to be corrected," Mitchell said.His concerns deepened recently when he observed approximately nine graves being dug over a weekend, leading him to question whether space truly is as limited as the city has indicated."As you can see, those were the graves that were dug and now they're covered up," Mitchell said.City points to mausoleum constructionThe city is pointing to the construction of a $2,875,010 mausoleum as a solution, which would add more than 2,000 spaces to the cemetery.Mitchell acknowledged the project but said it does not address the needs of everyone."It will be beautiful once it's completed, it's excellent. But until you have some residents that do not wish to be entombed, they wish to be interred," Mitchell said. "It's a solution but it's a bandaid to the overall problem."State lawmaker calls preservation a priorityState Rep. Rob Long, a former Delray Beach vice mayor, said the issues at the cemetery are serious and that preserving its history must be a priority."The issues at Delray Beach Memorial Gardens are serious, and preserving a cemetery that holds so much of Delray's history has to be a priority," Long said in a statement. "The State has already invested in documenting and preserving the site through the historic resource survey, and as the City works through what additional capital and preservation needs remain, I want to be at the table to help identify solutions and determine where the state may be able to assist through grants, appropriations, or other resources."Historic survey findings and what comes nextThe city commissioned LG2 Environmental Solutions to conduct a historic resource survey of the original section of the cemetery, funded through a State of Florida Small Matching Grant. The survey documented more than 1,200 historic graves, found that 94% of markers are in fair to poor condition, and recommended the site as potentially eligible for listing on the National Register of Historic Places.The report called for expanded fieldwork, improved landscaping practices, professional repairs and enhanced public outreach.The city said it expects to select a consultant this week to review operations and recommend improvements.Mitchell said he will keep pushing for accountability — including his call for a permanent on-site office at the cemetery."I will advocate until the sun goes down and the sun comes up that they put an office on site right here at the cemetery," Mitchell said.He said the fight is personal."It grieves me greatly to even have to deal with this and fight this fight, but I'm fighting it for my mother who is deceased," Mitchell said. "We as citizens need to make sure we're doing all that we can to make sure that they're being respected and that their wishes are being honored."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) ordered local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, and Treasure Coast law enforcement is responding to the decision.FDOT sent the memorandum on Monday, which came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology "out of control" last week.WATCH BELOW: Florida orders license plate reader removal; Treasure Coast reactsNot everyone disagrees with the move. Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras."I think it's an invasion of privacy," Reilly said. "I'm personally not a fan."But others in the community see the technology as a critical safety tool.Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe."I think it's super important to have that kind of technology out there to catch the bad guys," Bailey said.Neighbor Kristina Ramsey pointed to the cameras' track record."I definitely think it's helped catch a lot of criminals," Kristina said.Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised the license plate readers, like Flock cameras, after they aided in a homicide arrest last month."We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said.On Tuesday, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek responded directly to the state's removal decision."What's that do to the Martin County citizens? It makes us fundamentally less safe," Budensiek said.Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with the help of the cameras."We stopped and arrested President (Donald) Trump's would-be assassin. Last year, we stopped a kidnapper with two of our young girls headed to Nebraska. We stopped a traveling rooftop burglary crew," Budensiek said.Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said legislation, not removal, is the right path forward."Without those cameras out there on US-1, it's a needle in a haystack," Snyder said.Snyder called for a measured approach to address privacy concerns while preserving the public safety benefits."Meaningful legislation that regulates their use, protects privacy, but somehow allows us to keep the cameras and keep the community safe," Snyder said.Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record."If people still don't trust law enforcement, I would be OK with, and I believe the Florida sheriffs would be OK with, a public professional auditing system," Budensiek said.WPTV learned Tuesday that Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city. We're also learning on Tuesday, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will be limiting license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie Police Department has significantly limited the use of automated license plate reader technology after the Florida Department of Transportation issued a directive to remove certain cameras from state highway rights-of-way. 31, 2026, FDOT issued a memorandum revoking permits for license plate reader technology systems located within state highway rights-of-way and requiring affected equipment to be removed within 30 days. The PSLPD has seven cameras within FDOT rights-of-way that will be removed to comply with the directive. Effective immediately, the department is placing an operational pause on the use of its remaining automated license plate reader technology. Access to automated license plate reader technology systems during this pause will be limited to exigent circumstances involving an immediate threat to human life, such as cases involving a missing or endangered child, an endangered vulnerable adult, a homicide investigation with an immediate threat, or other situations where automated license plate reader technology information could prevent loss of life or great bodily harm. Every request to access automated license plate reader technology during the pause will require prior approval and authorization from Chief Leo Niemczyk. The PSLPD highlighted the effectiveness of automated license plate reader technology as an investigative tool, noting its role in locating missing people, recovering stolen vehicles, identifying suspects, developing leads and solving crimes. Since 2022, auto burglaries in Port St. Lucie have decreased by 17%, with automated license plate reader technology providing investigators an additional resource to protect the community. “This is a delicate balance. On one hand, we have a technology that has proven to be an important tool for our officers and investigators and has helped us protect people and solve crimes. On the other, we have a responsibility to listen to our community, respect the direction of our state leaders, and ensure our policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability and public safety. We are committed to finding that balance and doing what is right for the people we serve,” said Niemczyk. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro also sent out a press release on Tuesday updating their policy on the use of Automatic License Plate Reader Technology. Use of the technology will now require prior approval from the undersheriff and be limited to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered person investigations. Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods' attorney, Douglas Duncan , filed a notice Tuesday setting the hearing for 8:30 a.m. 2, before Judge Darren Steele at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart. The filing lists the subject of the hearing as a Change of Plea. The development marks a change from Woods' previous position in the case. In March , the 50-year-old golf legend entered a not guilty plea to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. It is not yet clear from the newly filed notice what plea Woods intends to enter Wednesday or whether the hearing is part of a negotiated plea agreement. See also: ' Rolling prison’: 2 women accused of heinous sexual abuse, neglect of 4 children The charges stem from a March 27 crash on South Beach Road on Jupiter Island. Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements. They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket, according to the arrest affidavit. Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case.

The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) ordered local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, and Treasure Coast law enforcement is responding to the decision.FDOT sent the memorandum on Monday, which came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology "out of control" last week.WATCH BELOW: Florida orders license plate reader removal; Treasure Coast reactsNot everyone disagrees with the move. Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras."I think it's an invasion of privacy," Reilly said. "I'm personally not a fan."But others in the community see the technology as a critical safety tool.Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe."I think it's super important to have that kind of technology out there to catch the bad guys," Bailey said.Neighbor Kristina Ramsey pointed to the cameras' track record."I definitely think it's helped catch a lot of criminals," Kristina said.Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised the license plate readers, like Flock cameras, after they aided in a homicide arrest last month."We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said.On Tuesday, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek responded directly to the state's removal decision."What's that do to the Martin County citizens? It makes us fundamentally less safe," Budensiek said.Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with the help of the cameras."We stopped and arrested President (Donald) Trump's would-be assassin. Last year, we stopped a kidnapper with two of our young girls headed to Nebraska. We stopped a traveling rooftop burglary crew," Budensiek said.Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said legislation, not removal, is the right path forward."Without those cameras out there on US-1, it's a needle in a haystack," Snyder said.Snyder called for a measured approach to address privacy concerns while preserving the public safety benefits."Meaningful legislation that regulates their use, protects privacy, but somehow allows us to keep the cameras and keep the community safe," Snyder said.Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record."If people still don't trust law enforcement, I would be OK with, and I believe the Florida sheriffs would be OK with, a public professional auditing system," Budensiek said.WPTV learned Tuesday that Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city. We're also learning on Tuesday, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will be limiting license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County could become a data center, according to a rezoning application sent to the city of Fort Pierce. Willow Lakes LLC, the owner of 203 acres of land off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, submitted a rezoning application in June to change 174 acres to light industrial use to allow for a data center. WATCH BELOW: New 203-acre data center proposed in St. Lucie County The rezoning application said, "the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial." Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area. "You have a beautiful view all the time," Whiteside said. When asked about the potential data center, her reaction was immediate. "I hate that idea," Whiteside said. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. "He was looking at what else he could potentially do at the property," Dobbins said. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. According to the rezoning application, the applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, "intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and/or restaurants/fast food." Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions. "Data centers are kind of the rage right now," Broderick said. Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. "If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said. The rezoning application said that if rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. According to the application, "the partner company would need to submit to the City a site plan application for the proposed data center and obtain City approval of the site plan." The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board on Sept.

Lucie homeowners are finding a flyer in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro , the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. According to the city's proposal, about 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit. One resident recounted her first reaction to getting the letter. I thought it was going to be money, not on my taxes, said Deborah Koon-Martin, a PSL homeowner. That difference is the part homeowners are most likely to notice when the notice arrives. Not every property qualifies for the larger amount. The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. You can use the money for other things. You're going to pay your taxes anyway, so it's not really helping, Koon-Martin said. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience. See also: West Palm Beach man arrested with gun at private school, police say When Koon-Martin was asked what she wanted from the city, her answer was clear. Because it makes it better. You have maggots crawling out of the trash. I’d rather go back to twice a week, said Koon-Martin. Council members also agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. "It's the taxpayers' money. The taxpayers were the ones who were wronged," Councilman Anthony Bonna said. The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Lucie's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Residents have continued pressing the city over once-a-week pickup, and the council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

Ed Markey of Massachusetts secured the Democratic nomination in his bid for a third term in office Tuesday, fighting off a challenger who argued that it was time for a generational change.Markey, 80, defeated U.S. Seth Moulton, 47, in the Senate primary.Moulton told voters it was time to do away with the “status quo.” Markey pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it was Moulton — not the older incumbent — who was out of touch with the state’s voters.Markey has boasted about his 2022 climate bill and called for an end to the war in Iran to bring down energy costs.In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle.Markey has been a fixture in Massachusetts politics since the 1970s and is seeking a third six-year term. Moulton, 47, repeatedly argued on the campaign trail that the Democratic Party is stuck in the “status quo” and questioned Markey’s accomplishments during his lengthy time in office.“People ought to ask, what are you going to accomplish in the next six years that you haven’t been able to accomplish in the last 50?” Moulton said.Markey pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it is Moulton — not the older incumbent — who is out of touch with Massachusetts voters. Markey boasted about his 2022 climate bill and called for an end to the war in Iran to bring down energy costs.He also sharply criticized Moulton for opposing “Medicare for All” — though Moulton has called for universal healthcare.“He has a backwards-looking political agenda,” Markey said.In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle, and the winner is expected to prevail in the general election in November.The Senate race was not the only generational challenge for Democrats on Tuesday's ballot. A similar dynamic played out in the 8th Congressional District, where Patrick Roath hoped to oust longtime incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, and in the 1st Congressional District of western Massachusetts, where progressive public school teacher Jeromie Whalen faced against Rep. Richard Neal.RELATED NEWS | 'Too late' for Trump to make major changes to how mail-in voting works, expert saysMoulton's comments on transgender children have been an issueDuring the campaign Markey repeatedly pointed out that Moulton, in 2024, raised eyebrows among some in the party for saying he did not want his daughters playing sports against transgender girls.Critics said he was echoing President Donald Trump’s talking points against allowing transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.Moulton has since apologized for his remarks, saying it was not his intention to hurt the transgender community and stressing his support for other transgender rights bills.“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”Moulton, who enlisted in the Marines after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and served four tours of duty in Iraq, was first elected to Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in 2014. He launched a 2020 presidential campaign but dropped it after a few months.Markey was elected to the Senate in 2013. Before that he represented Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District from 1976 to 2013.Markey notably fended off a challenge in 2020 from Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a younger rival from one of the nation's most famous political families. Markey did so by aligning himself with the liberal wing of the Democratic Party.Antoine Hilaire, a 76-year-old Democrat who voted for Markey in Brockton on Tuesday, said being older can be a positive because it offers people experience and wisdom.“If the older one is doing the better job, I don’t know,” he said. It’s not a big, big, big problem.”Longtime Democratic House incumbents also face younger challengersLynch, 71, has held the 8th District seat in south Boston since 2001. He faced Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer who contended that it is time to end “wait-your-turn” politics. Lynch stressed the value of experience inside Congress.Lynch has fended off other youth challenges in the past, but Roath’s campaign hoped for a boost of excitement after longtime Democratic incumbent U.S. John Larson was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in August in neighboring Connecticut. Like Roath, Bronin called for the need for generational change while running against an establishment politician.Meanwhile the 1st District primary in western Massachusetts pitted Neal, 77, against Whalen, 39.Neal, known as the dean of the New England House delegation, was first elected in 1988. Whalen ran to the left of Neal, calling for Medicare for All and questioning whether Neal has done enough to oppose Trump’s agenda.Whalen recently was endorsed by Our Revolution, a progressive organization founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

The Town of Jupiter is set to launch its first-ever municipal fire department on Oct. 1, ushering in a new era of public safety that connects back to a 70-year history of local service. The new Jupiter Fire Rescue agency will take over service from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, with many of its new firefighters having deep roots in the community they will now protect.WATCH: Jupiter's new municipal fire department prepares for Oct. 1 launchWith the transition just one month away, the new department marks a significant shift in emergency services for the town's residents and a return to a dedicated, Jupiter-focused fire service for the first time in nearly four decades.While this is the town's first government-run fire department, the history of firefighting in Jupiter began with volunteers more than 70 years ago."Back in 1950, we had a new chamber of commerce for Jupiter, and they realized one of the things that the community needed, as it was starting to grow post-World War II, is it needs some fire support," a local historian named Josh explained.That first department was a world away from modern fire rescue. It consisted of volunteers with no official uniforms, using converted military trucks and hand sprayers to protect their growing community. In 1985, these services were merged into the larger Palm Beach County Fire Rescue system.The new Jupiter Fire Rescue department is reviving the tradition of locals serving their own community. The department recently held a push-in ceremony for its first new fire engine and swore in its inaugural class of firefighters."Twenty-nine people that have joined Jupiter Fire Rescue are local hometown Jupiter people… and they have come home to serve their community," Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said.As they prepare for the official launch, the new crews are undergoing intensive training. Their preparation has also included learning more about the community's history, including a recent visit to the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, according to the historian.On Oct. 1, the new department will begin writing the next chapter of Jupiter's history, responding to calls from its new fire station and reviving a long-standing legacy of community-based service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. What began as a hit-and-run investigation in Palm City turned into a massive multi-agency manhunt Wednesday, ending with deputies pulling a suspect from a swamp along the Martin-St. CBS12 News was there as deputies emerged from the water with 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce in handcuffs. Both Daceus and the deputies who tracked him down were drenched from the murky swamp water after an hours-long search. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Daceus was wanted in connection with a hit-and-run crash in Palm City. Investigators say he fled the scene and ran through the Windstone community off Southwest Rivers End Way before disappearing into a large swampy area near the county line. His disappearance sparked a large-scale search involving Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, K-9 teams, aviation units, drone operators, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, and Port St. The search lasted more than two hours as helicopters circled overhead and officers established a perimeter around nearby neighborhoods. See also: One red-light camera ticket led to suspended license, criminal citation for PBC man "It's not an everyday occurrence," nearby resident and State Rep. Toby Overdorf told CBS12 News. The significant law enforcement presence forced the closure of parts of Southwest Murphy Road and temporarily prevented some residents from returning home. "With that kind of police presence, we felt we were okay," Overdorf said. The sheriff's office says the coordinated effort ultimately paid off, with technology playing a key role in locating Daceus. Court records reviewed Wednesday show Daceus previously had only a handful of traffic-related violations in Indian River County, including driving with a suspended license. Now, investigators say he could be facing far more serious charges. Despite the unusual scene unfolding near their homes, residents say they never doubted deputies would find the suspect. Martin County always gets their guy," Overdorf said. Daceus was being booked into the Martin County Jail Wednesday evening. Investigators are continuing to review the case and determine what charges he will ultimately face.

Two parked trucks were heavily damaged in a violent crash in Port St. Security video recorded the crash, which shows a black truck traveling at a high rate of speed on SW Lucero Drive around 3:40 p.m. The truck goes off the road into the grass and then slams into the two parked trucks. "When I heard the crash, I thought it was thunder," Elaine Harmon, a neighbor, said. "I heard a loud explosion," said another neighbor, Rocky Burkhead. "Thought it was just lightning like we've been having over the last few days." But when Burkhead stepped outside, he realized the situation was far worse than a weather-related incident. "I had no idea what to think. I was just at a loss for words. My first concern was, 'Is he OK?'" Burkhead said. Lucie police said the man in the black truck sustained only minor injuries. However, Burkhead said the damage to the two parked trucks hit in the collision was extensive. Both trucks belong to Burkhead and are essential for his pressure washing business. I had to rent a U-Haul today. You're limited on what you can do, how far you can go," Burkhead said. Neighbors said the crash is the most dramatic example of speeding on Southwest Lucero Drive but emphasized it is not an isolated incident. The speed limit on the road is 25 mph, but residents said drivers rarely adhere to it. "People do fly by on this road all the time," Courtney Gray, a neighbor, said. "There's a big problem with speeding on this road," Burkhead said. Residents are particularly concerned because the road lacks sidewalks, yet many people walk along it with children and pets. "I walk every day with (my baby) in the stroller or whatever. I'm just so thankful we weren't home when it happened," Gray said. "I think what they need to do is put some officers in the area, pull a few people over with some heavy-duty fines," Burkhead said. "Seems like something like this is going to keep happening if we don't have speed bumps," Gray said. Lucie police have not yet responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols. Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after firefighters quickly contained the blaze, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The fire was reported just after 6:30 a.m. in the 2700 block of Northeast Cypress Lane. When crews arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage of the home. According to the homeowner, a lithium-ion battery had been charging in the garage before the fire started. Firefighters immediately evacuated the residence and worked to contain the flames, preventing the fire from spreading beyond the garage. Officials said crews successfully extinguished the fire, and no neighboring structures were threatened. Fire rescue officials called the incident a close call and are reminding residents to follow proper lithium-ion battery safety practices. They encourage people to unplug batteries once they are fully charged to help prevent overheating and potential fires. hero.headline: Vero Beach man held on $1 million bond accused of using AI to create fake sexual images
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man is being held in the Indian River County Jail on a $1 million bond after police accused him of using artificial intelligence to create and distribute fake sexual images of real women without their consent. Peter Ruma downloaded pictures from social media and used AI prompts to remove women's clothing and place them in sexual situations, police said. Authorities said Ruma then distributed the images without the consent of the individuals depicted.

Police said Ruma has been engaging in this activity for several years. He is currently being held in the Indian River County Jail.

Authorities are warning there could be more victims. Police are expected to provide an update this afternoon.

The case marks the latest criminal prosecution involving artificial intelligence technology used to create non-consensual sexual imagery. Police said Ruma obtained the original photographs from social media accounts belonging to the women he targeted.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office gives all clear after bomb threat evacuates Fort Pierce Central High School
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Bomb Team gave the all clear at around 3 p.m. Friday following comprehensive sweeps of Fort Pierce Central High School after a bomb threat forced an evacuation earlier in the afternoon. No devices were located, and the scene has been deemed safe. The area around the school was secured and evacuated at around 1 p.m. while personnel conducted their assessment, evaluation and investigation. Students were released from school and after school activities will resume as planned, according to Lydia Martin of St. Lucie County Public Schools.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office takes all threats seriously but noted the real-world consequences of false alarms. "We take everything serious, but, you know, those types of pranks cost the communities a lot of money and obviously school time when stuff like that happens," Del Toro said. "When those happen, we do follow do a thorough follow-up investigation, and if we can arrest somebody in those types of calls, we make sure we do that."

Parents rushed to the school to pick up their children following the evacuation. Angela Jones, who was there to pick up her son, described the moment she heard the news. "That's my only child. hero.headline: Fort Pierce Central High School given all clear after bomb threat prompts evacuation
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office gave the all clear at Fort Pierce Central High School on Friday afternoon after a bomb threat prompted evacuation of the campus. The sheriff's office bomb team conducted comprehensive sweeps and found no devices. The scene was deemed safe around 3 p.m. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro warned that hoax threats drain community resources and could result in arrests.

The area around Fort Pierce Central High School was secured and evacuated around 1 p.m. while personnel conducted their assessment, evaluation and investigation. Lydia Martin of St. Lucie County Public Schools said parents were notified of the threat. A second message was sent to parents confirming the school had been cleared by law enforcement. Students were released from school and after school activities will resume as planned.

Parents rushed to the school to pick up their children following the evacuation. Angela Jones, who was there to pick up her son, said her heart was shaking and she was nervous. Cleveland Jamison Jr., a freshman at Fort Pierce Central High School, said he was inside the school when the threat was made. He said everybody got scared, ran into the room and kids were calling their moms.

Sheriff Del Toro said his office takes all threats seriously but noted the real-world consequences of false alarms. He said those types of pranks cost the communities a lot of money and obviously school time. He said when hoax calls happen, the office conducts a thorough follow-up investigation, and if they can arrest somebody in those types of calls, they make sure they do that.

hero.headline: Vero Beach mother held without bond on child sexual battery charges after Michigan cybertip leads to Indian River County arrest
hero.body:
A Vero Beach woman is being held without bond on two sexual battery charges after an Internet Crimes Against Children investigation in Michigan led Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies to her home. Lisette Zamarripa, 28, was arrested Sept. 3 and charged with two counts of sexual battery and one count of electronic transmission of child sexual abuse material. The Florida Department of Children and Families took custody of her two children, a 1-year-old girl and a 2-year-old boy. Prosecutors intend to seek a grand jury indictment on two counts of capital sexual battery because of the children's ages, according to an arrest affidavit.

Michigan State Police received a National Center for Missing and Exploited Children cybertip involving alleged child sexual abuse material associated with a Kik account. Investigators obtained a search warrant for the account and found images and videos allegedly showing an adult woman engaging in sexual acts with two children, both her biological children, according to the affidavit. Michigan investigators identified the woman as Zamarripa after comparing material from the account with her Facebook profile. Michigan investigators also served a search warrant on Zamarripa's boyfriend, Kenneth Conkle, where he admitted to directing and recording the abuse. He confessed to separately abusing his own 1-year-old daughter.

Indian River County deputies went to Zamarripa's Vero Beach home after investigators believed the children could be in immediate danger. A family member confirmed Zamarripa was inside with her two children. Deputies said Zamarripa came outside with the children and was separated from them. After being advised of her rights, she allegedly admitted that she committed sexual acts involving both children during a FaceTime call with their biological father, who lives in Michigan. The affidavit says Zamarripa told detectives the acts had been discussed with the father beforehand and that she livestreamed at least one incident for him to view.

The children's biological father faces charges in Michigan including child sexual battery, four counts of production of aggravated child sexual abuse material, and five counts of using a computer to commit a crime. Florida charges against Conkle are pending. Deputies seized Zamarripa's cellphone, which she allegedly said was used to record the material. Bond was set at $500,000, cash or surety, on the electronic transmission charge. Her arraignment is scheduled for 9 a.m.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man held on $1 million bond accused of using AI to create fake sexual images
cards.teaser: Peter Ruma is accused of downloading photos from social media and using artificial intelligence to digitally remove clothing from images of women. Police said he distributed the fake sexual images without consent and has been doing so for several years.
cards.body:
Peter Ruma of Vero Beach is being held in the Indian River County Jail on a $1 million bond, accused of using artificial intelligence to create fake sexual images of real people. Police said Ruma downloaded pictures from social media and used AI prompts to remove women's clothing, placing them in sexual situations. hero.headline: Fort Pierce Central High School evacuated after bomb threat; sheriff's office finds no device, warns of cost of hoax calls
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Central High School was evacuated Friday afternoon after a bomb threat prompted a response by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Bomb Team. The area around the school was secured and evacuated at around 1 p.m. while personnel conducted their assessment, evaluation and investigation. The sheriff's office gave the all clear at around 3 p.m. following comprehensive sweeps. No devices were located, and the scene has been deemed safe.

Lydia Martin of St. Lucie County Public Schools said parents were notified of the threat. A second message was sent to parents confirming the school had been cleared by law enforcement. Students were released from school and after school activities will resume as planned.

Parents rushed to the school to pick up their children following the evacuation. Angela Jones, who was there to pick up her son, said the timing made the situation unsettling. "My heart was shaking, I was nervous. I can't believe this, on a Friday, too, with a long weekend coming up," she said. Cleveland Jamison Jr., a freshman at Fort Pierce Central High School, said he was inside when the threat was made. "Everybody got scared, everybody ran into the room and all the kids were going crazy—people were calling their moms," he said.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Del Toro said his office takes all threats seriously but noted the real-world consequences of false alarms. "We take everything serious, but, you know, those types of pranks cost the communities a lot of money and obviously school time when stuff like that happens," he said. "When those happen, we do follow do a thorough follow-up investigation, and if we can arrest somebody in those types of calls, we make sure we do that."

cards.headline: Man dies after being shot multiple times in Fort Pierce; three masked suspects flee scene
cards.teaser: A man died at a hospital after being shot multiple times in Fort Pierce. Witnesses reported seeing three masked males run from the area after the shooting.
cards.body:
A man died at a local hospital after being shot multiple times in Fort Pierce, and police are searching for three masked suspects who fled the scene. The shooting happened in September, and officers located the man suffering from multiple gunshot wounds before he was taken to the hospital, where he later died.

According to the preliminary investigation, the victim became involved in a verbal altercation with several individuals before shots were fired. A firearm was located near the victim, and multiple shell casings were recovered from the scene. Witnesses reported seeing three masked males run away from the area following the shooting.

Detectives are continuing to gather evidence and interview witnesses as they work to determine the circumstances surrounding the shooting. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at www.tcwatch.org.

cards.teaser: Deputies have taken a 17-year-old suspect into custody and recovered a short-barreled pistol following a shootout with a 15-year-old in a residential neighborhood. Video evidence confirms the two teens fired at each other in the middle of the street.
cards.body:
A 17-year-old suspect is in custody after a shootout with a 15-year-old in Indian River County, and deputies have recovered a short-barreled pistol believed to have been used in the incident. The 17-year-old was taken into custody Thursday morning following the Wednesday night shooting in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest. Kevin Jaworski with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office confirmed that investigators obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway.

The shooting occurred at around 7:30 p.m. Wednesday after deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out.

Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. Jaworski said the incident appears to be isolated and there is no threat to the community, but noted it was inherently dangerous because a car was hit, a house was hit, and anybody in those could have very well easily been hurt. The case remains under investigation.
cards.article_text: Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. "The car had to have been here, and he had to shoot like that, boom, boom, boom, boom," Pitts said. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting. Kevin Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. "So, my first thing that comes to my mind is, where did he get it? This is a short-barreled pistol, a rifle that he was shooting in the middle of the street," Jaworski said. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire. Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. "Yes, yes, between the 17-year-old and the 15-year-old, they were actively shooting at each other in the middle of the street," Jaworski said. Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. "This was between those two juveniles, so there’s no threat to the community at this point, but it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because, like I said, a car was hit, a house was hit, and if anybody was in those, they could have very well easily been hurt," Jaworski said. Pitts expressed frustration over the incident and called for action to prevent similar events in the future. "I say crime watch, but when everybody sees something wrong, they got to say something," Pitts said. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives. cards.headline: Indian River County schools warn parents after two non-credible 'Cat in the Hat' threats
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office and school district are warning parents about a viral social media trend featuring threatening images of the Cat in the Hat character after receiving two non-credible threats targeting middle schools.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office and School District of Indian River County issued warnings to parents after receiving two threats linked to a viral social media trend featuring menacing images of the Cat in the Hat character. The threats targeted Vero Beach Middle School and Sebastian River Middle School, and the sheriff's office determined both were non-credible. The principal of Vero Beach High School sent out a voicemail warning to parents.

Jaime Alberti, the director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County, said the trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, with some containing threats. Many of the images appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. Alberti said students could face criminal charges if they issue a specific threat on someone, and would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct.

Alberti urged parents to monitor their children's social media accounts. "Talk to your kids, make sure you're checking their social media, make sure you're involved in what they're posting. And be friends with them and their accounts. So you know what's happening and what they're posting on social media," Alberti said. She said many people are interpreting the posts as serious threats and calling police and the Fortify Florida tip line to report concerns.
cards.article_text: A disturbing social media trend featuring a menacing version of the beloved Dr. Seuss character The Cat in the Hat is prompting warnings from school districts and law enforcement agencies nationwide. The trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, and some containing threats. On the Treasure Coast, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said threats to schools there have so far been non-credible, but they’re sounding the alarm to students and parents. "Talk to your kids, make sure you're checking their social media, make sure you’re involved in what they're posting. And be friends with them and their accounts. So you know what's happening and what they're posting on social media," said Jaime Alberti, the director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County. Some of the images of the character appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. And though many of them are intended to be just memes or jokes, law enforcement officials said some people are taking it to the next level, including threatening language targeted at specific schools and communities. "When one kid thinks maybe [it’s] a joke, somebody else may be interpreting it not as a joke. And obviously context matters and everything when you post it online. So a lot of the folks that are reading this online are getting scared, and they're calling the police and they're calling in the Fortify Florida tip line to report, hey, I'm seeing this online. This is a concern," Alberti said. The School District of Indian River County said it has received two of these threats, one at Vero Beach Middle School and another at Sebastian River Middle School. The sheriff’s office said both are non-credible. The principal of Vero Beach High School also sent out a voicemail warning to parents. Administrators said students could face consequences if they are found to have issued a threat. "If it's specific, a specific threat on someone, they could be charged criminal charges. And if not, they would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct," Alberti said. Administrators are urging parents to frequently monitor their children’s social media accounts. cards.headline: Fellsmere woman, 75, wakes at 2:30 a.m. daily to feed stray cats, volunteers 60 hours a week at animal sanctuary
cards.teaser: Linn Stewart of Indian River County rises before dawn each morning to feed a colony of stray cats, then spends her days volunteering at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere. The sanctuary provides free pet food to food banks, veterans, and seniors while caring for animals left behind by elderly owners.
cards.body:
Linn Stewart, a 75-year-old Indian River County resident, starts her day at 2:30 a.m. driving through the dark to feed her colony of stray cats. After the predawn feeding, Stewart volunteers 60 hours a week at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere, a sanctuary for pets left behind by senior citizens who can no longer care for them.

The sanctuary operates a pet food pantry that provides free pet food to food banks, veterans, and senior citizen organizations. Stewart and other volunteers cut open large bags and portion the food into four-pound bags. The sanctuary also provides medical care and flea medications when donations allow.

Stewart, who lost both parents at age 30 and has little family nearby, said the work keeps her going. She has rescued animals all her life and now stops to help tortoises, turtles, and other wildlife she encounters. Stewart requires only four hours of sleep per night, a pattern she said began in childhood. Her dedication recently earned her recognition and a $525.25 award from Guardians.
cards.article_text: Linn Stewart, a 75-year-old resident of Indian River County, starts her day at 2:30 a.m., driving through the dark to feed her colony of stray cats, a routine that has become central to her life. "You're up at 2:30 every morning?" she was asked. "Umm hmm, a lot of times I'm out at 2:30 every morning," Stewart said. While most people are still asleep, Stewart is already hard at work caring for animals that have become like family to her. "I've only required four hours of sleep since I was little. I drove my parents crazy," she said. Her love for animals has been a lifelong passion. "I've always loved animals. I would bring home anything and everything," Stewart said. "Once I got involved with (For the Love of) Paws, I realized that there were so many cats running around that I would just take care of them." After feeding the cats, Stewart volunteers 60 hours a week at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere, a sanctuary for pets left behind by senior citizens who can no longer care for them. The organization also operates a pet food pantry, providing free pet food to food banks, veterans, and senior citizen organizations. "We have a cat group and a dog group, and we put them on the tables, and we cut open the bags and dump them in bins, and then what we do is we transfer them to 4-pound bags," Stewart said. Stewart said the sanctuary provides more than just food. We provide medical sometimes. We get the donations and provide flea medications if we have it. It's just something that is really needed and appreciated," she said. Having lost her parents at the age of 30 and with little family nearby, Stewart said giving back is what keeps her going. I would be finding something to do," she said. Her compassion extends beyond cats and dogs. "I've stopped and rescued tortoises, turtles. I stopped one time last week, there was a coyote that had gotten hit. I realized it was a coyote. I still called to have somebody pick it up," she said. Stewart’s dedication has not gone unnoticed. "Love for Paws is part of your family. Well, at Guardians, we live that as well. We'd like to welcome you to the Guardians family, and thanks for all you do. You're rooted in your community, and we love to celebrate that. So congratulations, $525.25 goes to you," she was told. For Stewart, her work is a source of purpose and joy. "It keeps me going," she said. "I'll probably just disappear one day, but other than that, I have no health issues right now. Knock on wood, but this keeps me going because I have love for the animals." If you live in Indian River County or are just passing through, don’t be surprised if you see Stewart lending a hand to the helpless. cards.headline: Fort Pierce police search for three masked males after fatal shooting
cards.teaser: A man died from multiple gunshot wounds after a verbal altercation in Fort Pierce. Police are searching for three masked males seen fleeing the scene.
cards.body:
A man died from multiple gunshot wounds after a shooting in Fort Pierce, and police are searching for three masked males witnesses saw running from the area. The shooting happened in September when officers found the man suffering from gunshot wounds. He was taken to a local hospital, where he died.

According to the preliminary investigation, the victim became involved in a verbal altercation with several individuals before shots were fired. A firearm was located near the victim, and multiple shell casings were recovered from the scene.

Detectives are continuing to gather evidence and interview witnesses as they work to determine the circumstances surrounding the shooting. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at www.tcwatch.org.

hero.headline: Driver airlifted after single-car rollover on I-95 southbound near High Meadows in Palm City
hero.body:
A driver was flown to the hospital by LifeStar with traumatic injuries Friday night after a single-car rollover crash on Interstate 95 southbound near the High Meadows exit in Palm City. Martin County Fire Rescue said the car crashed into a palm tree and rolled over onto its side. The crash occurred just after 6:15 p.m. near Mile Marker 102, near Florida's Turnpike.

Martin County Fire Rescue's special operations team extricated the driver from the overturned vehicle. No other vehicles were involved in the collision. The Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol also responded to the scene.

The nearest trauma center is HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, which is 26 miles north. The closest Level 1 trauma center is St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, about 38 miles south.

All lanes of Interstate 95 southbound have been reopened. Martin County Fire Rescue posted on Facebook that C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, LifeStar, Alert 1, Rescue 211, Rescue 231, Engine 21, Engine 22, EMS 2, and Battalion 2 3 responded to the crash.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Central High School cleared after bomb threat; Sheriff Del Toro vows charges
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Bomb Team gave the all clear at Fort Pierce Central High School on Friday afternoon after comprehensive sweeps found no devices following a bomb threat. Deputies secured and evacuated the area around the school at around 1 p.m. while personnel conducted their assessment, evaluation and investigation. The scene was deemed safe at around 3 p.m., and St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office will pursue charges against whoever made the threat.

"We take everything serious, but, you know, those types of pranks cost the communities a lot of money and obviously school time when stuff like that happens," Del Toro said. "When those happen, we do follow do a thorough follow-up investigation, and if we can arrest somebody in those types of calls, we make sure we do that."

Lydia Martin of St. Lucie County Public Schools said parents were notified of the threat and received a second message confirming the school had been cleared by law enforcement. Students were released from school and after school activities will resume as planned. Parents rushed to the school to pick up their children following the evacuation. Angela Jones, who was there to pick up her son, said her heart was shaking and she was nervous. "I can't believe this, on a Friday, too, with a long weekend coming up," Jones said.

Cleveland Jamison Jr., a freshman at Fort Pierce Central High School, said he was inside the school when the threat was made. "Everybody got scared, everybody ran into the room and all the kids were going crazy—people were calling their moms," he said. During the incident, the sheriff's office asked the public to avoid the affected area and follow all instructions from law enforcement and emergency personnel. Residents were also asked not to approach or handle any suspicious items and to report any additional concerns or suspicious activity by calling 911.

hero.headline: Vero Beach mother held without bond on capital sexual battery charges after Michigan cybertip leads to rescue of two toddlers
hero.body:
A Vero Beach mother is being held without bond on two sexual battery charges after a Michigan Internet Crimes Against Children investigation led Indian River County deputies to rescue her two toddlers from her home. Lisette Zamarripa, 28, was arrested Sept. 3 by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and faces two counts of sexual battery and one count of electronic transmission of child sexual abuse material. Prosecutors intend to seek a grand jury indictment on two counts of capital sexual battery because of the children's ages. The Department of Children and Families took custody of the children, a 1-year-old girl and a 2-year-old boy.

Michigan State Police received a National Center for Missing and Exploited Children cybertip involving alleged child sexual abuse material associated with a Kik account. Investigators obtained a search warrant for the account and found images and videos allegedly showing an adult woman engaging in sexual acts with the two children, both her biological children, according to an arrest affidavit. Michigan investigators identified the woman as Zamarripa after comparing material from the account with her Facebook profile. Indian River County deputies went to Zamarripa's Vero Beach home after investigators believed the children could be in immediate danger.

After being advised of her rights, Zamarripa allegedly admitted that she committed sexual acts involving both children during a FaceTime call with their biological father, who lives in Michigan. The affidavit states Zamarripa told detectives the acts had been discussed with the father beforehand and that she livestreamed at least one incident for him to view. Investigators said she initially denied one allegation but later identified the children in sanitized images shown to her and admitted the conduct described in the evidence. Deputies seized Zamarripa's cellphone, which she allegedly said was used to record the material.

Michigan investigators also served a search warrant on Zamarripa's boyfriend, Kenneth Conkle, where he admitted to directing and recording the abuse. He confessed to separately abusing his own 1-year-old daughter. The biological father of Zamarripa's children faces charges in Michigan including child sexual battery, four counts of production of aggravated child sexual abuse material, and five counts of using a computer to commit a crime. Florida charges against Conkle are pending. Zamarripa is being held with no bond on the two sexual battery charges, and bond was set at $500,000 on the electronic transmission charge. Her arraignment is scheduled for 9 a.m.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man held on $1 million bond accused of using AI to create fake sexual images of women from social media
cards.teaser: Peter Ruma is accused of downloading pictures from social media and using artificial intelligence to remove women's clothing and place them in sexual situations. Police said the activity spanned several years and expect more victims to come forward.
cards.body:
Peter Ruma of Vero Beach is being held in the Indian River County Jail on a $1 million bond, accused of using artificial intelligence to create fake sexual images of real people. Police said Ruma downloaded pictures from social media and used AI prompts to remove women's clothing, placing them in sexual situations. Authorities said Ruma then distributed the images without the consent of the individuals depicted.

Police said Ruma has been engaging in this activity for several years. Authorities are warning there could be more victims and are expected to provide an update this afternoon.

hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Bomb Team gave the all clear at around 3 p.m. Friday following comprehensive sweeps of Fort Pierce Central High School after a bomb threat prompted an evacuation. No devices were located, and the scene has been deemed safe, deputies said. The area around Fort Pierce Central High School was secured and evacuated at around 1 p.m., while personnel conducted their assessment, evaluation and investigation. Lydia Martin of St. Lucie County Public Schools said parents were notified of the threat, and a second message was sent to parents confirming the school had been cleared by law enforcement. Students were released from school and after school activities will resume as planned.

Parents rushed to the school to pick up their children following the evacuation. Angela Jones, who was there to pick up her son, said the timing made the situation even more unsettling. So, you know, I'm just like, okay, what do I do, you know? Yeah, very scary." "Everybody got scared, everybody ran into the room and all the kids were going crazy—people were calling their moms," he said.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office takes all threats seriously, but noted the real-world consequences of false alarms. "We take everything serious, but, you know, those types of pranks cost the communities a lot of money and obviously school time when stuff like that happens," he said. "When those happen, we do follow do a thorough follow-up investigation, and if we can arrest somebody in those types of calls, we make sure we do that."

During the incident, the sheriff's office asked the public to avoid the affected area and follow all instructions from law enforcement and emergency personnel. Residents were also asked not to approach or handle any suspicious items and to report any additional concerns or suspicious activity by calling 911.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested for allegedly hitting mother of his children with car, dragging her on hood during custody dispute
cards.teaser: Brandon Isaiah Martin was arrested on an outstanding warrant charging him with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon after deputies say he struck the mother of his children with a Kia Soul and drove several houses with her on the hood. A judge issued a protective order prohibiting contact.
cards.body:
Brandon Isaiah Martin, 24, of Port St. Lucie was arrested September 2 on an outstanding warrant charging him with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon after deputies say he struck the mother of his children with a vehicle and drove several houses down the street while she was on the hood during an April 28, 2025, incident on 26th Court Southwest in Vero Beach. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office warrant identifies a motor vehicle as the alleged weapon. A judge approved the warrant May 5, 2025, and set Martin's bond at $50,000.

Deputies said the woman went to the home after a friend told her Martin was there removing property. The woman told deputies Martin was attempting to leave with their two children. The pair had joint custody but no formal custody documentation, according to the probable cause affidavit. As the woman was placing one of the children into another vehicle, Martin allegedly drove a silver Kia Soul toward her and struck her, causing her to land on the hood, deputies wrote.

The woman told deputies Martin continued driving with her on the hood for about four or five houses. She said she heard him threaten to kill her, according to the affidavit. The vehicle stopped after Martin's mother, who was in the front passenger seat, put it in neutral, deputies said. The woman was able to get off the hood and told deputies she feared for her life. A witness told deputies she saw Martin drive toward the woman, strike her and continue down the street with the woman still on the hood. Deputies documented abrasions to the woman's knees. The order prohibits Martin from contacting the woman and requires him to stay specified distances away from her, her home, workplace and vehicle. Deputies served Martin with the warrant at a Vero Beach address on September 2. Jail records show he later posted bond.
