cards.headline: Former DeSantis spokesperson's PR firm secures more than $700,000 in Florida government contracts
cards.teaser: Former GOP communications director Taryn Fenske has secured more than $700,000 in government contracts through her PR company since 2023. State records show the DeSantis administration has been a steady client after Fenske launched her private firm.
cards.body:
State records show that over the past three years, former GOP communications director Taryn Fenske has secured more than $700,000 in government contracts through her PR company, TMF Communications. Fenske built her political career in Tallahassee, working for Gov. Rick Scott, the Republican National Committee and Education Commissioner Richard Corcoran. By 2021, she was part of Governor Ron DeSantis' executive communications team and eventually worked for his presidential super PAC. After DeSantis' presidential run ended, Fenske launched her own private PR firm.

Since 2023, TMF Communications has been awarded five- and six-figure state contracts for PR consulting work across multiple agencies, according to the state's government contract database. New College has paid TMF more than $400,000 for PR consulting work since 2023. The Agency for Persons with Disabilities hired TMF to help rebrand the agency for $75,000 in 2025. The Department of Children and Families budgeted $113,000 for TMF to support digital media vendors in 2025. Florida's Department of Health allocated nearly $40,000 to TMF earlier this year, and another $52,000 was allocated to the firm in 2026.

Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, said the amount is exorbitant and that the arrangement looks like Fenske is being rewarded for her service to the DeSantis administration. DeSantis' current communications director, Alex Lanfranconi, called TMF's state business awesome and described Fenske as one of the best communications professionals in the state. Fenske called questions over whether her loyalty to the DeSantis administration contributed to her state work insulting and dismissive of her professional qualifications, saying her company's work was earned on its merits.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested for using AI to create fake sexual images of women
hero.body:
Vero Beach police arrested Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, on eight criminal charges after he used artificial intelligence to create and distribute sexually explicit altered images of women without their consent. Ruma faces three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. He is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond.

Detectives determined Ruma used AI to create sexually explicit altered images depicting victims without their consent and then distributed or promoted those images. Ruma used photographs obtained from social media and other online sources to create some of the altered images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said. Detectives executed search warrants on Ruma's residence and electronic devices during the investigation, and a forensic examination of those devices resulted in the recovery of evidence associated with the creation and distribution of altered sexual images.

The current charges stem from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 and relate to one female victim. During the investigation, detectives identified several additional females believed to have been victimized through similar conduct. Investigators also have information indicating Ruma may have engaged in this type of conduct for several years. Vero Beach Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared. The investigation also uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years.

Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver. Currey stressed that investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665. Additional charges may be forthcoming as additional victims or evidence are identified.

cards.headline: Man found incompetent to stand trial in random stabbing death of Stuart woman
cards.teaser: A Martin County judge ruled that Kersten Francilus, 25, charged with fatally stabbing 73-year-old Joyce Ellen Thompson Adams in the Southwood community near Stuart, is incompetent to stand trial.
cards.body:
A Martin County judge ruled that Kersten Francilus, 25, charged with fatally stabbing 73-year-old Joyce Ellen Thompson Adams in the Southwood community near Stuart, is incompetent to stand trial. Francilus was examined by two doctors and determined to be incompetent during a hearing in August. He has been remanded to a state mental hospital for restoration to competency before his case can proceed. Francilus faces premeditated first-degree murder charges in the April 2025 stabbing death of Adams.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit reveals Adams was stabbed more than 50 times, far more than the approximately 16 to 17 times initially reported. The first responding deputy arrived at the intersection of Southeast Black Oak Lane and Woods Edge Trail and witnessed Francilus stabbing Adams in the neck and back. Francilus dropped the knife and complied with commands to get on the ground when ordered by deputies at gunpoint. First responders transported Adams to the Cleveland Clinic South Emergency Room, where she was pronounced dead.

Investigators spoke with Francilus' mother, who confirmed the serrated knife used in the attack came from their home. She told detectives she usually stored the knives above the microwave to hide them from her son. The mother also revealed her son had not taken his prescribed medication since February 2025. Francilus told investigators he admitted himself into a mental health facility at Coral Shores shortly before the stabbing, but investigators are still working to confirm that claim. During an interview with investigators, Francilus admitted to leaving his residence and said he did what he did.

He has been remanded to a state mental hospital for restoration to competency before his case can proceed.Francilus faces premeditated first-degree murder charges in the April 2025 stabbing death of Joyce Ellen Thompson Adams in the Southwood community near Stuart. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit reveals the attack was far more brutal than initially reported.While investigators previously said Adams was stabbed approximately 16 to 17 times, they now believe she was stabbed more than 50 times."Unfortunately, it's even worse than what I described the other day," Sheriff John Budensiek said.According to the affidavit, the first responding deputy arrived at the intersection of Southeast Black Oak Lane and Woods Edge Trail and witnessed Francilus stabbing Adams in the neck and back. Francilus dropped the knife and complied with commands to get on the ground when ordered by deputies at gunpoint.First responders transported Adams to the Cleveland Clinic South Emergency Room, where she was pronounced dead.Before the fatal stabbing, multiple residents reported a man matching Francilus' description walking through the Southwood neighborhood, approaching homes and asking about a nearby bank. Callers noted he appeared "out of it.""Yeah, he was knocking on doors, and most, I guess, everybody you know, just kept their door closed," neighbors Peter Burke and Lori Soo said.The affidavit reveals one resident told investigators the man came to her house asking for a bank. When she opened the door, he attempted to step inside, but she shut the door and alerted her husband.Sheriff Budensiek said Francilus specifically targeted women, asking whether their husbands were home, and approached two children in an open garage."He asked multiple ladies if their husbands were home. All of which responded yes and closed the door," Budensiek said. "We have two kids that were in an open garage door where he asked them if the kids' parents were home and they turned around and — thankfully — ran inside and shut the door. This could have been a lot worse."This tragedy highlights ongoing concerns about mental health resources and intervention in Florida communities. The case underscores the critical importance of mental health treatment compliance and the challenges families face when loved ones refuse medication.Investigators spoke with Francilus' mother, who confirmed the serrated knife used in the attack came from their home. She told detectives she usually stored the knives above the microwave to hide them from her son.The mother also revealed her son had not taken his prescribed medication since February 2025."He was on types of psychotropic medications for psychological problems," Budensiek said. "He was off the meds just because he didn't want to take them."The Martin County Sheriff's Office said Francilus had two prior encounters with law enforcement in 2025. One involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and resulted in Francilus being Baker Acted.In September 2025, Francilus' mother called the Martin County Sheriff's Office to report her son was hearing voices."The voices telling him to go here, go there," Budensiek said. "Our deputies got there, asked him if he was suicidal, 'no,' 'Do you want to hurt anyone?' 'No,' so at that point we didn't have enough to Baker Act him."Budensiek added that Francilus told deputies he had admitted himself into a mental health facility at Coral Shores shortly before that interaction, but investigators are still working to confirm that claim.During an interview with investigators, Francilus admitted to leaving his residence and said he "did what I did."When asked to describe Adams, Francilus said she was Jewish. However, the affidavit shows investigators spoke with Adams' daughter, who confirmed her mother was not Jewish. When asked if anything about her mother could lead someone to think she was Jewish, the daughter provided a brief response: "Possibly her appearance."Budensiek said nothing currently indicates Francilus was antisemitic, but detectives are working to determine whether that belief played a role in why Adams was targeted.A neighbor who wished to remain anonymous said he had spoken with Francilus before the stabbing and thought he seemed like he "wasn't all there" but was talking normally. He then heard screams and found Adams covered in blood, recognizable only by her shoes he had seen her wearing around the neighborhood.The neighbor tried to pull Francilus away but said Francilus was too heavy and did not appear to notice him. Francilus stopped only when deputies arrived and ordered him to the ground at gunpoint.Another neighbor said the situation was terrible but that at least Adams "is with her husband now," referring to her husband, who passed away 10 to 15 years prior."So we don't know of any motive," Budensiek said. "At this point, we don't know of any nexus between the victim and the suspect. We simply know that we've had a horrendous crime that's taken place in this neighborhood."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Two teens fired at each other in Indian River County shootout, deputies say
hero.body:
Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire.

Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. Kevin Jaworski, a spokesman for the sheriff's office, confirmed the exchange. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting. Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. The weapon was described as a short-barreled pistol rifle.

Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. Jaworski said the shooting was between the two juveniles and there is no threat to the community at this point, but noted it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because a car was hit and a house was hit, and anyone in those locations could have easily been hurt.

Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives.

Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. "The car had to have been here, and he had to shoot like that, boom, boom, boom, boom," Pitts said. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting. Kevin Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. "So, my first thing that comes to my mind is, where did he get it? This is a short-barreled pistol, a rifle that he was shooting in the middle of the street," Jaworski said. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire. Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. "Yes, yes, between the 17-year-old and the 15-year-old, they were actively shooting at each other in the middle of the street," Jaworski said. Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. "This was between those two juveniles, so there’s no threat to the community at this point, but it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because, like I said, a car was hit, a house was hit, and if anybody was in those, they could have very well easily been hurt," Jaworski said. Pitts expressed frustration over the incident and called for action to prevent similar events in the future. "I say crime watch, but when everybody sees something wrong, they got to say something," Pitts said. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman charged in alleged $57 million IRS tax refund fraud scheme
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS, according to the U.S. Justice Department. A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering.

Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said.

Chandler, Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho, and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, according to prosecutors. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds.

The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. An indictment is an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

cards.headline: Teen arrested within 24 hours in Fort Pierce armed robbery, police say
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old is accused of setting up an armed robbery in Fort Pierce on Wednesday in which three suspects confronted a victim who had arranged an online meetup.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is accused of setting up an armed robbery in Fort Pierce, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department. On Wednesday, officers responded to an armed robbery in which the victim arranged an online meetup and was confronted by three males.

One suspect displayed an AR-15-style rifle and stole the victim's iPhone, according to FPPD. The other suspects stole a purse and other personal belongings from the victim's grandmother's vehicle.

During the investigation, detectives quickly identified a 16-year-old male as one of the suspects involved in the robbery. Within 24 hours of the crime, detectives located and arrested the 16-year-old, according to FPPD.

hero.headline: Palm City woman pleads not guilty to 72 charges in Border Collie hoarding case, surrenders dogs for adoption
hero.body:
Paige O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from the rescue of 36 Border Collies from her Palm City home earlier this month and legally surrendered the dogs for adoption. Martin County court records show O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls it the worst animal hoarding case in its history.

The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's home on Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on missed trash collection and old seafood.

The rescued Border Collies underwent medical grooming, a process involving carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said staff shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine. Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, investigators found lots of pieces of metal, rusted metal, sharp metal that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass, according to Fisher.

The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay and neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups. The shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time to keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services. The case has prompted State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, to push for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.

The legal surrender clears the path for the rescued dogs to find new homes after undergoing medical evaluations and rehabilitation.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs to WPTV, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions. Potential adopters will receive clear information about any long-term medical needs the animals may have.The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups.The shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time to keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services. All applicants will undergo extensive vetting to ensure appropriate matches between dogs and families.This case highlights the growing problem of animal hoarding in Florida and has prompted legislative action, including a push for mandatory dog breeder registries. The successful rescue and rehabilitation of these 36 Border Collies demonstrates how communities can respond to animal neglect while providing pathways for recovery and adoption.The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris.Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process involving carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, investigators found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass," according to Fisher.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal. Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. hero.headline: DeSantis pledges to campaign for Amendment 3 as local leaders warn of service cuts and fee hikes
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. Under the amendment's ballot language, the expanded exemption would not apply to school district taxes. The proposal would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including businesses and rental properties, from 10 percent to 5 percent, and restrict how counties and municipalities use property-tax revenue. DeSantis said he has not settled on how he will participate and would not lead a political committee's statewide fundraising effort, but added he would be involved because he thinks the amendment is important.

The governor rejected warnings from local leaders that the amendment would leave communities unable to provide basic services. DeSantis said he would support state funding to help rural counties with limited tax bases absorb revenue losses, though any state assistance would depend on lawmakers approving the funding. Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava launched a South Florida campaign Wednesday to defeat Amendment 3, joined by local leaders, labor organizations and business and civic groups. She warned that communities could face service cuts, higher fees or some combination of both, and said Miami-Dade could lose about 10 percent of its general fund revenue in the first year and 20 percent in the second.

Levine Cava said renters and businesses could shoulder additional costs without receiving the expanded homestead exemption. Supporters have potentially encouraging polling numbers. A Sachs Media survey conducted August 18 randomly assigned 800 Florida voters to groups reviewing either the original ballot language or a court-ordered revision. Support was 65 percent among those who read the revised wording, compared with 60 percent among those who saw the original. The difference was not statistically significant.

The Florida Policy Institute estimates that public hospital districts and health systems would lose approximately $323 million over three years under Amendment 3. The institute warns that reduced funding could affect staffing, access to care and programs serving uninsured and underinsured patients. Amendment 3 requires approval from at least 60 percent of voters casting ballots on the measure in November. If approved, it would take effect in January.

cards.headline: Thieves target Florida SNAP recipients, use stolen benefits to buy baby formula at California address
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Florida families reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California, with most purchases for baby formula known to be resold on the black market.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Florida families have reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California. A majority of the purchases are for baby formula, which is known to be resold on the black market. After reaching out to DoorDash multiple times, the Tampa Bay 28 I-Team confirmed that nearly all of the purchases being made at the Glendale, California address are for baby formula.

Victims described the financial toll of the theft. Shayna Houser Parra told the I-Team that she and her family still have not had all of their bills covered because of the theft. Cheyanne Smith said she has gone through three cards and that locks, canceling the card and changing her PIN have not worked. In July, one of the Florida victims posted the address the SNAP fraud is tied to in a Facebook group for DoorDash drivers in California. Someone responded, writing that they had delivered formula there like two or three times and each time it was like five to seven cans.

The Glendale Police Department said it has received more calls from Florida law enforcement agencies since the I-Team's previous report, as its investigation continues. The Department of Children and Families has given no indication it is doing anything to investigate the fraud, instead directing people to contact law enforcement and increase the security on their accounts. Records show the U.S. Government Accountability Office also wanted to know what is being done to prevent SNAP benefit theft. However, there is no requirement for state agencies to report data on stolen benefits to the federal government. That authority ended in 2024, along with the Stolen SNAP Benefits Program that reimbursed victims of fraud, meaning the benefits stolen from families will not be returned.

A majority of the purchases, the I-Team discovered — are for baby formula, which is known to be resold on the black market. Victims described the financial toll of the theft."We still haven't had all of our bills covered this month because of this. It's either eat or pay bills," Shayna Houser Parra told the I-Team. WATCH: Thieves stealing SNAP benefits from Florida families are using the tax dollars to buy baby formulaOthers described the frustration of trying to secure their accounts without success."I've went through three cards. The locks, the canceling of the card, the changing my PIN — nothing worked, because they're just messing with it over and over again," Cheyanne Smith said.In July, one of the Florida victims posted the address the SNAP fraud is tied to in a Facebook group for DoorDash drivers in California. Someone responded, writing: "I've delivered formula there like 2 or 3 times and each time it's like 5-7 cans. Usually a lady comes and gets it or I leave it at the gate."After reaching out to DoorDash multiple times, since the grocery orders were delivered through that platform, the I-Team confirmed that nearly all of the purchases being made at the Glendale, California address are for baby formula — a commodity with a well-documented black market.A sampling of recent cases help to illustrate the scope of the problem:Last year, 19 people were charged in Oregon for stealing SNAP cards around the country and "using the money to purchase baby formula which was then sold on the black market."In California, a woman was arrested for fraudulent SNAP card transactions. Deputies then recovered more than 100 cases of baby formula last year. In May, a California couple was sentenced to federal prison for helping coordinate the shipping of stolen baby formula worth more than $2 million.A DoorDash spokesperson told the I-Team the company is responding to the investigation."We are actively investigating this issue and are prepared to cooperate with law enforcement requests to assist their investigation and help resolve the issue for these families." The I-Team has also contacted the Florida Department of Children and Families, Florida's Chief Financial Officer, the State Attorney General's Office, the FBI, the USDA and the Glendale Police Department.The Glendale Police Department said it has received more calls from Florida law enforcement agencies since the I-Team's previous report, as its investigation continues.DCF has given no indication it is doing anything to investigate the fraud, instead directing people to contact law enforcement and increase the security on their accounts, saying the agency is "actively working to further strengthen safeguards for recipients."Records show the U.S. Government Accountability Office also wanted to know what is being done to prevent SNAP benefit theft. However, there is no requirement for state agencies to report data on stolen benefits to the federal government. That authority ended in 2024, along with the Stolen SNAP Benefits Program that reimbursed victims of fraud — meaning the benefits stolen from families will not be returned. Victims say the state's response falls short."We're not the only people and the state's not wanting to help us, so my question is — why is the state just so willing to lose money?" Houser Parra said.DCF says SNAP recipients can visit a Department Family Resource Center to add a security code to their account, which is separate from their PIN. Families in contact with the I-Team say the added security code, so far, has been effective.DCF also recommends updating to the latest version of the app ebtEDGE to access the newest security features.

cards.headline: Former DeSantis spokesperson's PR firm secures more than $700,000 in state contracts
cards.teaser: Former GOP communications director Taryn Fenske has secured more than $700,000 in government contracts through her PR company, TMF Communications, since launching the firm after DeSantis' presidential run ended.
cards.body:
State records show that over the past three years, former GOP communications director Taryn Fenske has secured more than $700,000 in government contracts through her PR company, TMF Communications. Fenske built her political career in Tallahassee, working for Governor Rick Scott, the Republican National Committee and Education Commissioner Richard Corcoran. By 2021, she was part of Governor Ron DeSantis' executive communications team and eventually worked for his presidential super PAC. After DeSantis' presidential run ended, Fenske launched her own private PR firm and state contract records show the DeSantis administration has been a steady client.

Since 2023, TMF Communications has been awarded five- and six-figure state contracts for PR consulting work across multiple agencies. Earlier this year, Florida's Department of Health allocated nearly $40,000 to TMF. In 2025, the Department of Children and Families budgeted $113,000 for TMF to support digital media vendors. In 2025, the Agency for Persons with Disabilities hired TMF to help rebrand the agency for $75,000. In 2026, another $52,000 was allocated to the TMF. Since 2023, New College has paid TMF more than $400,000 for PR consulting work. State contract records also show that in 2023, the state Justice Administration Commission paid TMF nearly $27,000 to assist with PR after Governor DeSantis suspended Orange County State Attorney Monique Worrell.

Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, reviewed the findings and said that to the average citizen, the average taxpayer, that is an exorbitant amount of money. DeSantis' current communications director, Alex Lanfranconi, called TMF's state business awesome, describing Fenske as one of the best communications professionals in the state. Fenske declined to speak on camera. In an email, she called the premise of a question over whether her loyalty to the DeSantis administration contributed to her state work insulting and dismissive of her professional qualifications. She also said her company's work was earned on its merits.

hero.headline: Vero Beach police expect more charges, victims in AI-generated sexual image case
hero.body:
Vero Beach police say they expect more charges against a man accused of creating and sharing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent, and they believe additional victims have yet to be identified. Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that the current eight charges against 37-year-old Peter Solomon Ruma involve one adult female victim. Ruma is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond.

Ruma is charged with three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. Investigators said the victim came forward after discovering her image had been altered. Detectives searched Ruma's home and seized two phones, and a forensic review of the devices produced evidence that advanced the investigation.

Police said Ruma allegedly used photographs of real women, including images from social media and other publicly available online sources, to make the altered sexual images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said. Currey said investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared.

Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver. Currey stressed that investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Police also said the investigation uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman among 7 charged in alleged $57M IRS tax refund fraud scheme
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie woman is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money.
cards.body:
A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering. Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said.

Chandler, Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho, and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

cards.headline: Woman facing 72 charges in Palm City dog hoarding case pleads not guilty after surrendering animals
cards.teaser: Paige O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case in its history, while legally surrendering the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered by O'Donnell, clearing the way for adoptions. According to Martin County court records, O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions.

The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on missed trash collection and old seafood. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said staff shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine. Fisher said some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur.
cards.article_text: Paige O'Donnell has pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case in its history, while legally surrendering the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home for adoption.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW:According to Martin County court records, O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The legal surrender clears the path for the rescued dogs to find new homes after undergoing medical evaluations and rehabilitation.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs to WPTV, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions. Potential adopters will receive clear information about any long-term medical needs the animals may have.The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups.The shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time to keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services. All applicants will undergo extensive vetting to ensure appropriate matches between dogs and families.This case highlights the growing problem of animal hoarding in Florida and has prompted legislative action, including a push for mandatory dog breeder registries. The successful rescue and rehabilitation of these 36 Border Collies demonstrates how communities can respond to animal neglect while providing pathways for recovery and adoption.The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris.Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process involving carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, investigators found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass," according to Fisher.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal. Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."Perea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under Florida law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Indiantown Village Council fires manager, appoints former Stuart city manager as interim
hero.body:
The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had been in the role since 2023, during a meeting originally called to discuss a moratorium on data centers. The council appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager following Kryzda's dismissal. Giardino was recently fired as Stuart city manager.

Giardino said he was approached by two council members about the position. He attended the special meeting where the council made its decision. Giardino said it appeared to him that the voters wanted a change in Indiantown and that the village council received that information.

Kimberly Jackson Brown, a 59-year resident of Indiantown, said the decision was a step in the right direction because the biggest change has to be to have the trust of the people for the council. She said if the village has a council that residents can trust, then all the changes can be enacted.

The meeting also addressed data centers, which has sparked debate within the community. After hearing public input, the council rejected a resolution to pause data center development and instructed its new legal counsel to revise the proposal's language. The data center issue will return to the council for further discussion.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested for using AI to create fake sexual images of women, held on $1 million bond
hero.body:
A 37-year-old Vero Beach man was arrested Wednesday on eight charges after investigators say he used artificial intelligence to create and distribute sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Peter Solomon Ruma faces three counts of creation of an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person, three counts of promotion of an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person, one count of sexual cyberharassment, and one count of stalking. He is being held at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office on a $1 million bond.

Detectives with the Vero Beach Police Department executed search warrants on Ruma's residence and electronic devices during the investigation. A forensic examination of those devices resulted in the recovery of evidence investigators believe is associated with the creation and distribution of altered sexual images. Photographs obtained from social media and other online sources were used to create some of the altered images, according to police.

The current charges stem from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 and relate to one female victim. During the course of the investigation, detectives identified several additional females believed to have been victimized through similar conduct. Investigators also have information indicating Ruma may have engaged in this type of conduct for several years. Court records show Ruma has a prior criminal history in Indian River County, with a 2007 arrest on charges that included burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person, and a 2009 burglary charge that resulted in a sentence to the Florida Department of Corrections.

Detectives believe there may be additional victims who have not yet been identified or who may be unaware that altered sexual images depicting them were created or distributed. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized by Ruma, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding altered or sexually explicit images allegedly created or distributed by Ruma, is encouraged to contact Detective Matakaetis of the Vero Beach Police Department at (772) 978-4665. Those wishing to remain anonymous can contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477 and may be eligible for a cash reward. The investigation remains ongoing, and additional charges may be forthcoming as additional victims or evidence are identified.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County votes to remove license plate readers from county roads over privacy concerns
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners voted Tuesday to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-owned roads and property, while also halting the issuance of new permits and potentially revoking existing ones. The vote follows earlier restrictions imposed by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office limiting license plate reader use to forcible felony investigations and missing person cases.

The motion, introduced by Commissioner James Clasby, passed 3-2. Commissioner Erin Lowry said during the meeting, "I feel like everywhere you turn now in our community is a Flock camera." Clasby emphasized the need to protect residents' privacy, saying, "And I believe that we need to protect our citizens and order the removal from our right-of-way. It's actually mind-boggling. It's almost impossible to go anywhere without being tagged by at least one."

Commissioner Cathy Townsend and another member voted against the measure, expressing a desire for input from local law enforcement before making a decision. Commissioner Jamie Fowler questioned the handling of data collected by the cameras during the discussion. In July, Paris Lewbel, a spokesperson for Flock Safety, explained that data collected by the cameras is controlled by the agency using them and is deleted after 30 days by default. Every search within the Flock platform is recorded in an immutable audit log, which tracks who conducted the search, the reason, and the parameters.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro released a statement saying his office would comply with the state order to remove cameras from state highways and tighten internal rules but did not call for their removal from county roads. Port St. Lucie Police Chief John Bolduc also announced an operational pause on automated license plate readers. The decision by the county commissioners goes beyond the Florida Department of Transportation's directive to remove cameras from state highways, extending the removal to county-controlled public rights of way.

hero.headline: Body found in Martin County mangroves confirmed as missing visitor from Oklahoma
hero.body:
Martin County authorities confirmed that a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island is that of Michael Anthony Debevec, who was reported missing last week after visiting Chastain Beach. Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office found Debevec's body Tuesday after an extensive search of the area. Detectives reported they have not found any apparent signs of foul play. The Medical Examiner has not yet determined Debevec's cause of death.

The search began after a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to Debevec's home in an attempt to return it, prompting his family to report him missing. Investigators later found Debevec's vehicle at Chastain Beach, more than two miles from where his body was ultimately discovered.

Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators determined Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed Debevec's phone was in use Friday morning and moving between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge, according to investigators.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. The Martin County Sheriff's Office thanked the community members who shared information about Debevec and helped with the search. Debevec's family has been notified of his death.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man held on $1 million bond for creating AI deepfake sexual images
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man was arrested Wednesday and is being held on a $1 million bond after creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without consent. Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, faces eight charges stemming from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 relating to one female victim. The charges include three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting those depictions, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Officers with the Vero Beach Police Department say Ruma took photos from social media and other online sources to create some of the altered images. Investigators searched Ruma's home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence connecting back to the creation and distribution of the AI-generated images. An arrest warrant was obtained after the investigation.

Police have identified several additional potential victims who have not been identified or may not know images of them were created or shared. Investigators also believe Ruma may have engaged in this conduct for years. Court records show Ruma has a prior criminal history in Indian River County. In 2007, he was arrested on charges that included burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. In 2009, he was arrested on a burglary charge and was later sentenced to the Florida Department of Corrections.

Investigators are publicly urging anyone who believes they may have been victimized, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding the altered or explicit images, to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. The investigation is still ongoing, and additional charges could be filed. Federal officials recently launched TakeItDown.FTC.gov, a resource that allows victims to report nonconsensual intimate images and seek their removal from online platforms.

hero.headline: Former St. Lucie GOP chairman arrested in Martin County for harvesting saw palmetto berries at public parks
hero.body:
Former St. Lucie County Republican Executive Committee Chairman Kenneth Ford Nail was arrested in Martin County after deputies said he harvested saw palmetto berries from public parks in Jensen Beach and Palm City without a permit authorizing the locations. A Martin County sheriff's deputy stopped Nail's gray Kia Soul on Aug. 25 near Southwest Murphy Road and Southwest Island Way in Palm City after a records check showed the temporary tag was unassigned and had expired five days earlier. The deputy saw a bundle of saw palmetto berries in the car and cutting shears on the front passenger seat.

Nail told deputies he had picked berries at parks in Jensen Beach and Palm City and had more berries in the rear hatch area. He said he had a Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services permit for his mother's property, but asked whether he could also pick berries on public land. Deputies said the permit applied only to the address listed on it. He was arrested on a charge of harvesting palmetto berries without a permit or landowner permission. Deputies photographed the berries and returned them to nature.

Nail, 57, was chairman of the St. Lucie County Republican Executive Committee in 2023 and early 2024. He was among local Republicans who publicly called for then-Gov. Ron DeSantis appointee, Sheriff Keith Pearson, to resign over an FDLE investigation into the 2020 sheriff's race. The affidavit says Nail was held without bond because he was already out on bond in a case alleging the introduction of contraband into a correctional facility.

In April 2025, Nail was arrested at Okeechobee Correctional Institution after deputies alleged that legal documents he was attempting to serve on an inmate concealed cellphones, chargers, and alprazolam. Nail denied knowing the contraband was inside the documents, the report said.

cards.headline: Multi-vehicle crash blocks I-95 southbound near Kanner Highway in Martin County
cards.teaser: A multi-vehicle crash that occurred Tuesday night blocked all southbound lanes of I-95 near Kanner Highway in Martin County, injuring four people.
cards.body:
A multi-vehicle crash blocked all southbound lanes of I-95 near Kanner Highway in Martin County on Tuesday night. The Martin County Sheriff's Office, Martin County Fire Rescue and Florida Highway Patrol responded to the crash, which occurred just before 8 p.m. The crash occurred very close to a motorcycle crash from earlier in the day.

Martin County Fire Rescue said paramedics treated one patient with traumatic injuries and three more with minor injuries. Crews quickly extinguished a fire that had started in one of the five vehicles involved, and paramedics assessed those in need. The southbound lanes remained closed following the crash.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested on $1 million bond in AI deepfake sexual images case
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man arrested Wednesday after creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent is being held on a $1 million bond. Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, faces eight charges related to one female victim stemming from incidents occurring between June and August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting those depictions, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Vero Beach Police Department officers searched Ruma's home and electronic devices Wednesday and found evidence connecting him to the creation and distribution of the AI-generated images. Investigators say Ruma took photos from social media and other online sources to create the altered images. Police have identified several additional potential victims who have not been identified or may not know images of them were created or shared. Investigators believe Ruma may have engaged in this conduct for years.

Court records show Ruma has a prior criminal history in Indian River County. In 2007, he was arrested on charges that included burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. In 2009, he was arrested on a burglary charge and was later sentenced to the Florida Department of Corrections.

Investigators are urging anyone who believes they may have been victimized, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding the altered or explicit images, to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. Federal officials recently launched TakeItDown.FTC.gov, a resource that allows victims to report nonconsensual intimate images and seek their removal from online platforms.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce felon arrested with 33 pounds of marijuana, $150K cash and guns in drug bust
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives arrested a convicted felon Wednesday morning after seizing 33 pounds of marijuana, more than $150,000 in cash, and multiple firearms at a Fort Pierce home.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Division detectives, assisted by the agency's SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant Wednesday morning at a residence in the 700 block of Cedar Place. Investigators arrested 59-year-old Stacy Tyrner of Fort Pierce without incident. During the search, detectives seized approximately 33 pounds of marijuana and more than $150,000 in cash, along with multiple firearms.

Investigators also found boxes of ammunition matching the calibers of the firearms, additional gun parts and components, drug paraphernalia, packaging materials, a currency counter, and other items they say were consistent with the sale and distribution of narcotics. According to the sheriff's office, Tyrner is a convicted felon and is prohibited from possessing firearms. Tyrner was charged with sale/delivery of a controlled substance stemming from a warrant arrest, trafficking in marijuana, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, and possession of drug paraphernalia.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro praised the Special Investigations Division, SWAT Team, and U.S. Marshals Service for their work in removing what he described as drugs, illegal firearms, and illicit cash from the community. Del Toro said this is another step toward the goal of making St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida.

cards.headline: Indian River County schools warn parents about viral 'Cat in the Hat' threat trend
cards.teaser: The School District of Indian River County received two threats tied to a nationwide social media trend featuring a menacing version of the Dr. Seuss character, prompting warnings to students and parents.
cards.body:
The School District of Indian River County received two threats tied to a viral social media trend featuring a menacing version of the Dr. Seuss character The Cat in the Hat. The threats targeted Vero Beach Middle School and Sebastian River Middle School. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said both threats are non-credible.

The trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, some containing threats. Some images appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. Law enforcement officials said some people are adding threatening language targeted at specific schools and communities. The principal of Vero Beach High School sent out a voicemail warning to parents.

Jaime Alberti, director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County, said students could face consequences if they are found to have issued a threat. Students making specific threats could be charged with criminal charges and would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct. Administrators are urging parents to frequently monitor their children's social media accounts.
cards.article_text: A disturbing social media trend featuring a menacing version of the beloved Dr. Seuss character The Cat in the Hat is prompting warnings from school districts and law enforcement agencies nationwide. The trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, and some containing threats. On the Treasure Coast, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said threats to schools there have so far been non-credible, but they’re sounding the alarm to students and parents. "Talk to your kids, make sure you're checking their social media, make sure you’re involved in what they're posting. And be friends with them and their accounts. So you know what's happening and what they're posting on social media," said Jaime Alberti, the director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County. Some of the images of the character appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. And though many of them are intended to be just memes or jokes, law enforcement officials said some people are taking it to the next level, including threatening language targeted at specific schools and communities. "When one kid thinks maybe [it’s] a joke, somebody else may be interpreting it not as a joke. And obviously context matters and everything when you post it online. So a lot of the folks that are reading this online are getting scared, and they're calling the police and they're calling in the Fortify Florida tip line to report, hey, I'm seeing this online. This is a concern," Alberti said. The School District of Indian River County said it has received two of these threats, one at Vero Beach Middle School and another at Sebastian River Middle School. The sheriff’s office said both are non-credible. The principal of Vero Beach High School also sent out a voicemail warning to parents. Administrators said students could face consequences if they are found to have issued a threat. "If it's specific, a specific threat on someone, they could be charged criminal charges. And if not, they would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct," Alberti said. Administrators are urging parents to frequently monitor their children’s social media accounts. hero.headline: Fort Pierce felon arrested with 33 pounds of marijuana, $150K cash and guns in drug bust
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives arrested a convicted felon Wednesday morning after seizing 33 pounds of marijuana, more than $150,000 in cash, and multiple firearms at a Fort Pierce home in the 700 block of Cedar Place. Investigators from the Special Investigations Division, assisted by the agency's SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant and arrested 59-year-old Stacy Tyrner of Fort Pierce without incident.

During the search, detectives found boxes of ammunition matching the calibers of the firearms, additional gun parts and components, drug paraphernalia, packaging materials, a currency counter, and other items consistent with the sale and distribution of narcotics. Tyrner is a convicted felon and is prohibited from possessing firearms.

Tyrner was charged with sale/delivery of a controlled substance stemming from a warrant arrest, trafficking in marijuana, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, and possession of drug paraphernalia. Sheriff Richard Del Toro praised the Special Investigations Division, SWAT Team, and U.S. Marshals Service for their work in removing what he described as drugs, illegal firearms, and illicit cash from the community.

"Drugs destroy lives and fuel crime, and we will not allow criminals to profit from that destruction," Del Toro said. "This is another step toward our goal of making St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida."

hero.headline: Indiantown council rejects pause on data center projects, will seek new legal opinion
hero.body:
Indiantown council members voted 4-1 against pausing data center applications Tuesday, opting instead to seek a new legal opinion and lawsuit-proof language before taking action. The vote came after hours of public comment from residents divided over whether hyperscale data centers belong in the rural village.

Carroll McAlister, who has lived in Indiantown her whole life, said she worries about what large-scale development means for the community. She said she fears data centers would accelerate that change. Other residents echoed her concerns during the meeting, with one saying they do not support taking agricultural land away. Not everyone opposed the projects. One speaker urged the council to keep options open, while another argued the developments could benefit the village if handled correctly.

During the meeting, an attorney for Silver Fox 606, a proposed data center project in Indiantown, threatened to sue if the village moved to pause data center projects. Concerns over the language of the proposed resolution was ultimately why council members opted to seek additional legal guidance before acting. Some residents left the meeting feeling cautiously optimistic that the village could still find a path forward. Resident Eric Miller said there is a common ground that says they need to take a pause if they are going to put 12 million more square feet of roof in the town.

The data center debate came during a turbulent meeting for Indiantown leadership. Just two weeks after three new council members unseated incumbents, the city manager was fired, the city attorney resigned, and Michael Giardino was named interim city manager just one week after losing his city manager job in Stuart.

cards.headline: Martin County authorities confirm body found in mangroves is missing Oklahoma visitor
cards.teaser: Deputies confirmed that a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge is that of Michael Anthony Debevec, who was reported missing last week after visiting Chastain Beach.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office confirmed that a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge is that of Michael Anthony Debevec, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing last week. Investigators say they found Debevec's body Tuesday after an extensive search of the area around Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island. Detectives reported that they have not found any apparent signs of foul play. The Medical Examiner has not yet determined Debevec's cause of death.

The search began after a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec. The person went to Debevec's home in an attempt to return it, prompting his family to report him missing. Investigators later found Debevec's vehicle at Chastain Beach, more than two miles from where his body was ultimately discovered.

Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators determined Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. August 27, and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed Debevec's phone was in use Friday morning and moving between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body.

cards.headline: Tiger Woods' license suspension raises questions about golf cart use in Martin County
cards.teaser: When Tiger Woods received his 5-year drivers license suspension Wednesday in his plea agreement for a March crash on Jupiter Island, questions immediately arose about whether he can still drive a golf cart.
cards.body:
Tiger Woods received his 5-year drivers license suspension in his Wednesday plea agreement for a March crash on Jupiter Island, raising questions about whether he can still drive a golf cart. Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said in a news conference that he would have to look into it. Bakkedahl said he knows you cannot drive a golf cart while impaired on the roads because it is a vehicle, adding that his gut reaction is going to be no.

In Florida, golf carts are considered low speed vehicles with speeds of 20-25 miles per hour and generally need title, registration and insurance and be driven by a licensed driver. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said to his knowledge, Tiger Woods would be allowed to drive a golf cart onto the golf course in his private golf community, but when it comes to driving the cart on public roads or in places where you see people driving on in areas that are open to the public, he would suggest Woods avoids doing that.

Aronberg cautioned testing the rules of the plea agreement. He said if there is a gray area, stay away from that. You do not want any risk of going back in front of the judge and having to explain yourself why you may or may not have violated your probation.

hero.headline: Indiantown council rejects one-year pause on data center applications
hero.body:
Indiantown council members voted 4-1 Tuesday against pausing data center applications, choosing instead to seek a new legal opinion and lawsuit-proof language before taking action. The vote came after hours of public comment from residents divided over whether hyperscale data centers belong in the rural village.

Carroll McAlister, who has lived in Indiantown her whole life, said she worries about what large-scale development means for the community. She said she fears data centers would accelerate the loss of the village's rural lifestyle. Other residents voiced similar concerns, with one saying they do not support taking agricultural land away for data centers. However, some residents urged the council to keep options open, arguing that smart development could improve lives in Indiantown if zoned appropriately.

During the meeting, an attorney for Silver Fox 606, a proposed data center project in Indiantown, threatened to sue if the village moved to pause data center projects. Concerns over the language of the proposed resolution was ultimately why council members opted to seek additional legal guidance before acting. One council member said the council's responsibility is to understand both what the law prevents them from doing and what authority remains available to the village.

The data center debate came during a turbulent meeting for Indiantown leadership. Just two weeks after three new council members unseated incumbents, the city manager was fired, the city attorney resigned, and Michael Giardino was named interim city manager just one week after losing his city manager job in Stuart. Some residents left the meeting feeling cautiously optimistic that the village could still find a path forward, with resident Eric Miller saying there is common ground that a pause is needed to ensure governmental infrastructure can handle 12 million more square feet of roof in the town.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested for creating AI deepfake sexual images, held on $1 million bond
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man was arrested Wednesday and is being held on a $1 million bond after creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, faces eight charges stemming from incidents between June and August 2026 involving one female victim, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting those depictions, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of stalking.

Vero Beach Police Department officers searched Ruma's home and electronic devices Wednesday and found evidence connecting him to the creation and distribution of the AI-generated images. Officers say Ruma took photos from social media and other online sources to create the altered images. Police identified several additional potential victims who may not know images of them were created or shared. Investigators believe Ruma may have engaged in this conduct for years.

Court records show Ruma has prior criminal history in Indian River County. In 2007, he was arrested on charges including burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. In 2009, he was arrested on a burglary charge and was later sentenced to the Florida Department of Corrections.

Investigators are urging anyone who believes they may have been victimized, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding the altered or explicit images, to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. Federal officials recently launched TakeItDown.FTC.gov, a resource that allows victims to report nonconsensual intimate images and seek their removal from online platforms.

cards.headline: Tiger Woods accepts Martin County plea deal, loses license for five years after Jupiter Island crash
cards.teaser: Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to reckless driving Tuesday in Martin County, avoiding a DUI conviction but losing his driver's license for five years.
cards.body:
Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to reckless driving Tuesday in Martin County under a plea deal that reduced the charge from DUI. Woods must pay a $1,500 fine and surrender his driver's license for five years. Deputies arrested Woods in March after his SUV rolled over on Jupiter Island.

Investigators determined Woods caused the crash and arrested him on suspicion of driving under the influence. Authorities later added a second charge after Woods refused to provide a urine sample that could have determined whether he had drugs in his system. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said the lack of chemical test results created significant challenges for prosecutors. Video showing Woods appearing unsteady after the crash was not necessarily enough to prove impairment, and the defense could have argued Woods's condition resulted from the rollover and his history of injuries.

Under the agreement, Woods may not operate a vehicle on public roads during the five-year suspension. Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said Woods likely cannot drive a golf cart on public roads because it is considered a vehicle, though he may operate one on private property.
cards.article_text: Tiger Woods will not face a DUI conviction after accepting a plea deal Tuesday that reduced the charge against him to reckless driving. Woods pleaded no contest to the lesser charge in Martin County. Under the agreement, the professional golfer will avoid jail but must pay a $1,500 fine and surrender his driver’s license for five years. Deputies arrested Woods in March after his SUV rolled over on Jupiter Island. Investigators determined Woods caused the crash, and deputies arrested him on suspicion of driving under the influence. Authorities later added a second charge after Woods refused to provide a urine sample that could have determined whether he had drugs in his system. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said the lack of chemical test results created significant challenges for prosecutors and would have been difficult if this went to trial. “This was not a slam-dunk case. What you have is video of him acting a little unsteady after a rollover accident. So, could use that in his defense," explained Aronberg said video showing Woods appearing unsteady after the crash was not necessarily enough to prove impairment. The defense could have argued Woods’ condition resulted from the rollover and his history of injuries. Under the agreement, Woods may not operate a vehicle on public roads during the five-year suspension. That restriction includes driving a golf cart on a public road, although he may operate one on private property. “It resolves a matter that would have taken up a lot of time, a lot of energy, a lot of bandwidth, and also was no guarantee,” Aronberg said. Aronberg said he does not believe Woods received favorable or harsher treatment because of his fame. He said prosecutors had to weigh the available evidence and that the agreement represented a fair resolution for both sides.
