cards.headline: Indian River County schools warn parents about viral 'Cat in the Hat' threat trend
cards.teaser: The School District of Indian River County received two threats related to a viral social media trend featuring a menacing version of The Cat in the Hat, though the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said both are non-credible.
cards.body:
The School District of Indian River County received two threats related to a viral social media trend featuring a menacing version of the Dr. Seuss character The Cat in the Hat. One threat targeted Vero Beach Middle School and another Sebastian River Middle School. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said both threats are non-credible.

The trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, some containing threats. Some images appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. Law enforcement officials said some people are taking the trend to the next level, including threatening language targeted at specific schools and communities. The principal of Vero Beach High School sent out a voicemail warning to parents.

Jaime Alberti, the director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County, said students could face criminal charges if they issue specific threats, and would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct. Administrators are urging parents to frequently monitor their children's social media accounts.
cards.article_text: A disturbing social media trend featuring a menacing version of the beloved Dr. Seuss character The Cat in the Hat is prompting warnings from school districts and law enforcement agencies nationwide. The trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, and some containing threats. On the Treasure Coast, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said threats to schools there have so far been non-credible, but they’re sounding the alarm to students and parents. "Talk to your kids, make sure you're checking their social media, make sure you’re involved in what they're posting. And be friends with them and their accounts. So you know what's happening and what they're posting on social media," said Jaime Alberti, the director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County. Some of the images of the character appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. And though many of them are intended to be just memes or jokes, law enforcement officials said some people are taking it to the next level, including threatening language targeted at specific schools and communities. "When one kid thinks maybe [it’s] a joke, somebody else may be interpreting it not as a joke. And obviously context matters and everything when you post it online. So a lot of the folks that are reading this online are getting scared, and they're calling the police and they're calling in the Fortify Florida tip line to report, hey, I'm seeing this online. This is a concern," Alberti said. The School District of Indian River County said it has received two of these threats, one at Vero Beach Middle School and another at Sebastian River Middle School. The sheriff’s office said both are non-credible. The principal of Vero Beach High School also sent out a voicemail warning to parents. Administrators said students could face consequences if they are found to have issued a threat. "If it's specific, a specific threat on someone, they could be charged criminal charges. And if not, they would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct," Alberti said. Administrators are urging parents to frequently monitor their children’s social media accounts. cards.teaser: Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said he will need to research whether Tiger Woods can drive a golf cart following his five-year driver's license suspension.
cards.body:
Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said he will need to research whether Tiger Woods can drive a golf cart following the five-year driver's license suspension Woods received in his Wednesday plea agreement for a March crash on Jupiter Island. Bakkedahl said in a news conference that golf carts are considered vehicles and his gut reaction is Woods cannot drive one on public roads.

In Florida, golf carts are considered low speed vehicles with speeds of 20 to 25 miles per hour and generally need title, registration and insurance and must be driven by a licensed driver. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said Woods would be allowed to drive a golf cart onto the golf course in his private golf community, but should avoid driving the cart on public roads or in places open to the public.

Aronberg cautioned testing the rules of the plea agreement. He said Woods should stay away from gray areas to avoid any risk of going back in front of the judge and having to explain why he may or may not have violated his probation.

hero.headline: Viral AI-generated Cat in the Hat threat targets Vero Beach High School, deemed not credible
hero.body:
A threatening AI-generated Cat in the Hat post targeted Vero Beach High School as part of a viral nationwide wave of similar school threats, but the Indian River County Sheriff's Office says the threat is not credible. The sheriff's office said there are no credible threats to Indian River County schools or students at this time.

Deputies are investigating the trend, monitoring social media activity and coordinating with the School District of Indian River County to help ensure campus safety. The sheriff's office announced on Facebook that any student found to have participated in the activity could face discipline under the Code of Student Conduct and potentially criminal charges.

The warning comes as law enforcement agencies nationwide respond to a viral trend involving AI-generated images of the Cat from the 2003 live-action Cat in the Hat movie starring Mike Myers. USA TODAY reported that the trend, initially described as a prank intended to scare people online, has prompted some school districts to increase security or cancel classes out of an abundance of caution. Authorities in communities including Louisville, Kentucky, Falfurrias, Texas, and Hanover County, Virginia, have also issued warnings about posts referencing schools or individual students.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is urging anyone who sees threatening content involving local schools or students to report it to law enforcement rather than sharing it. The sheriff's office emphasized that while the current posts reviewed locally have not been deemed credible, all threats involving school safety are being taken seriously.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police pause license plate readers citywide
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police have paused the use of 126 license plate readers throughout the city, limiting the technology to circumstances where there is an immediate threat to human life. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk announced the operational pause in response to community concerns about privacy.

Niemczyk said the pause aims to find a path forward that preserves public trust while maintaining an effective crime-fighting tool. He said the readers take pictures of the rear of vehicles and are not used for traffic enforcement, red light enforcement, or speeding enforcement. The technology does not use biometrics or facial recognition.

The police chief said the technology has delivered measurable results, including a 17% reduction in auto burglaries and a reduction in traveling crime. Residents remain divided on the issue. Joseph Hamm said he thinks the readers are great, while Peter Schmitt called them a privacy invasion that should be illegal.

Niemczyk said he wants lawmakers in Tallahassee to get answers from manufacturers like Flock about data retention and work with legislators to provide usage guidelines that protect both the community and officers. He said the technology has made police more effective but acknowledged the need to balance that benefit with community trust.

cards.headline: Body recovered from Martin County mangroves identified by clothing as missing Port St. Lucie man
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office recovered a body Tuesday morning from mangroves near the House of Refuge believed to be Michael Anthony Debevec, who was reported missing after a Good Samaritan found his wallet and returned it to his family.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office recovered a body Tuesday morning from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island believed to be Michael Anthony Debevec, a Port St. Lucie man who was reported missing after last being seen at Chastain Beach on Aug. 26. The deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing, though decomposition made it impossible to determine cause of death, according to Sheriff John Budensiek.

The missing person report was filed after a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, prompting his family to contact authorities. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered.

Detectives determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. on August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found.

hero.headline: Tiger Woods avoids DUI conviction in Martin County crash, state attorney defends plea deal
hero.body:
Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to reckless driving and refusal to submit to a lawful test Wednesday in Martin County Court in connection with his March 27 rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods was sentenced to a $1,000 fine for reckless driving, a $500 fine for the refusal charge, and an additional fine for careless driving. His license was suspended for five years.

Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl held a press conference Wednesday to defend his office's handling of the case, explaining that two toxicologists consulted by both the prosecution and defense concluded there was insufficient evidence to prove Woods was impaired by hydrocodone. The toxicologists examined police reports, deputy descriptions of Woods' behavior, body camera videos, and pharmacy records. They found no signs of impairment that would warrant prosecution under the legal standard required for controlled substance DUI cases. Woods' documented tolerance to the medication due to long-term use following multiple back surgeries further complicated the case.

The March crash occurred when Woods, driving his Range Rover at high speed, attempted to overtake a pickup truck hauling pressure-cleaning equipment. He clipped the trailer, causing his SUV to flip onto its side. Neither driver was injured. Woods' refusal to provide a urine sample at the scene constituted a separate criminal offense. Bakkedahl described the plea negotiations as mutually assured destruction, noting that while his office was confident they could prove the refusal charge, other evidence challenges made the DUI prosecution uncertain.

If Woods had been convicted on the original charges, he could have faced up to one year in county jail for the reckless driving second offense and 60 days for the refusal charge. Bakkedahl said he made decisions based upon his oath, his ethical responsibility, and his personal morals. When asked about public criticism of the plea deal, Bakkedahl said he did what he thinks is right. This marks Woods' second DUI-related legal issue in Florida. In 2017, he was arrested in Palm Beach County and later pleaded guilty to reckless driving as part of a plea deal.

cards.headline: Motorcycle crash shuts down I-95 southbound in southern Martin County near Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: A motorcycle crash closed all southbound lanes of I-95 near mile marker 98 in southern Martin County on Tuesday, and the driver was airlifted to a hospital with traumatic injuries.
cards.body:
A motorcycle crash closed all southbound lanes of I-95 near mile marker 98 in southern Martin County on Tuesday evening. The crash took place just north of Hobe Sound and Exit 96 at Bridge Road, and south of Exit 101 at Kanner Highway in Stuart, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol. The driver of the motorcycle was flown to a nearby hospital.

Martin County Fire Rescue said the crash happened just before 7 p.m. Firefighters worked to extinguish heavy flames from the bike while paramedics assessed the driver. LifeStar was called in to airlift the driver to the hospital with traumatic injuries. The lanes were reopened, only to be closed once again just a little while after thanks to another crash.

hero.headline: Florida orders removal of license plate cameras from state highways within 30 days
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation issued an Aug. 31 directive revoking approvals for automated license plate readers within state highway rights-of-way and ordering local law enforcement agencies to remove the devices within 30 days. After that period, FDOT will remove any covered cameras that remain. The department is also stopping new approvals, citing the rapid growth of camera networks, reports of misuse and concerns about data privacy.

The order covers license plate readers from different manufacturers, including Flock Safety. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records. The directive applies to cameras on state highways but does not automatically cover cameras on local roads and private property outside FDOT's jurisdiction.

Gov. Ron DeSantis has questioned who controls the information collected by the cameras and what safeguards prevent abuse. Florida officers have faced accusations of using the databases to track spouses or former partners, national outlets reported. DeSantis pointed to New Hampshire as a possible model for restrictions on roadside readers while preserving their use in police vehicles. New Hampshire's law defines a license plate reader as a device mounted to a vehicle and attended and operated by a law enforcement officer.

Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said the county's readers help solve serious crimes but would be taken down following the governor's order, according to the Miami Herald. Democratic state Rep. Anna Eskamani of Orlando supported FDOT's decision but said it leaves cameras operating on city streets, county roads and private properties, including neighborhood entrances and shopping centers. Eskamani urged Central Florida governments to pause new contracts and publish an accounting of existing systems, including how many cameras are deployed, who can search their records, how long information is kept and whether it is shared with agencies outside Florida. DeSantis said Monday he was unsure legislative leaders could reach an agreement on broader restrictions quickly, while leaving open the possibility of action after the election and before he leaves office in January.

cards.headline: Data centers become battleground in Florida governor's race as candidates split on AI infrastructure
cards.teaser: Republican nominee Byron Donalds argues that data centers are infrastructure Florida needs to compete, while Democratic nominee David Jolly wants a one-year pause on construction to examine environmental, health and economic consequences.
cards.body:
Republican nominee Byron Donalds has outlined three priorities for regulating data centers: protecting customers from higher utility bills, limiting water demands through cooling systems that recirculate water or use air, and keeping facilities away from homes. His campaign says local communities should be able to reject the facilities. Democratic nominee David Jolly wants Florida to stop new construction while questions about impacts are examined. He says he would impose a one-year statewide moratorium beginning when he takes office if elected.

A July University of North Florida poll found 68% of likely Florida voters opposed an AI data center in their local area, while 28% supported one. The survey of 848 likely midterm voters was conducted July 8-17 and had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. A national Economist/YouGov poll conducted in August found 66% of adults opposed a new data center in their community, compared with 19% who supported one. That national survey also found 60% believed a new data center would increase their electricity costs.

Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a law in May that preserves local authority over development and requires utility rate protections designed to ensure large data centers cover their own cost of service. It also establishes water-permitting requirements. The law calls for an independent study of data centers' economic, environmental, energy and public health effects.
cards.article_text: The data cloud needs a place to land. Florida's candidates for governor disagree on the welcome mat.Republican nominee Byron Donalds argues that data centers are infrastructure Florida needs to compete, with safeguards to protect water supplies, electric customers and nearby neighborhoods. Democratic nominee David Jolly wants a one-year pause on construction to examine the environmental, health and economic consequences.WATCH BELOW: Data centers divide Florida governor's raceTheir disagreement is turning the buildings behind artificial intelligence into a campaign battle over familiar concerns: what happens to Florida's land and water, who benefits from development and who gets the bill."Well, what happens when you threaten capital is capital leaves," Donalds said in an interview.He argues that discouraging investment could undermine the economic opportunities Floridians need to keep up with the cost of living."People need to be able to afford the Florida dream and build for their lives. But you can't build for your life if you don't have a high-paying job. And you're not going to have a high-paying job if you don't have companies who invest in your state," Donalds said.Donalds has outlined three priorities for regulating the facilities: protecting customers from higher utility bills, limiting water demands through cooling systems that recirculate water or use air, and keeping facilities away from homes.His campaign also says local communities should be able to reject them."If communities don't want data centers, there will be no data centers in those communities, "the campaign said in a statement reported by Florida Politics.Florida has already adopted new restrictions. Ron DeSantis in May, preserves local authority over development and requires utility rate protections designed to ensure large data centers cover their own cost of service. It also establishes water-permitting requirements.The law calls for an independent study of data centers' economic, environmental, energy and public health effects.Jolly wants Florida to stop new construction while questions about those impacts are examined. He says he would impose a one-year statewide moratorium beginning when he takes office if elected."They are rushing to build these things for reasons of profit for the industry, but not out of public interest, and I think we need to hit pause," Jolly said.His campaign is making Donalds' support for the projects an advertising target, telling viewers to "Say no to Data Center Donalds.”The White House, meanwhile, wants the accelerator.President Donald Trump argued Monday that data centers bring jobs and lower taxes, warning that communities rejecting them could end up "backwards and poor." His administration has also promoted a ratepayer protection pledge calling on major technology companies to cover the energy and infrastructure costs of their projects.But that sales pitch faces a skeptical audience.A July University of North Florida poll found 68% of likely Florida voters opposed an AI data center in their local area, while 28% supported one. The survey of 848 likely midterm voters was conducted July 8–17 and had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points.A national Economist/YouGov poll conducted Aug. adults opposed a new data center in their community, compared with 19% who supported one. Opposition included 71% of Democrats, 66% of independents and 52% of Republicans.That national survey also found 60% believed a new data center would increase their electricity costs.The polls measured attitudes toward local construction, not support for a statewide moratorium. Still, they show the political challenge facing supporters of expansion.The promise is an economic boom. Many voters remain unconvinced they want it moving in next door.

cards.headline: Governor's race candidates propose different approaches to license plate camera restrictions
cards.teaser: Republican nominee Byron Donalds has backed the camera removals and additional reforms, while Democratic nominee David Jolly has called for a warrant requirement.
cards.body:
Republican nominee Byron Donalds supported the governor's move to remove cameras from state highways in an interview on Fox Business, according to Florida Politics. Democratic nominee David Jolly has called for a warrant requirement, while saying any new rules must preserve law enforcement's ability to respond to crimes in progress. Jolly renewed his call for a special session Monday, urging lawmakers to address the issue sooner.

Automated readers photograph passing vehicles and capture information police can search to locate suspects, stolen cars or missing people. The privacy concern is that the cameras also collect information about motorists who are not suspected of a crime. Flock told Fox Business it supports stronger safeguards while preserving technology it says helps police solve crimes and find missing people.
cards.article_text: Florida's license plate cameras are collecting something besides tag numbers: bipartisan pushback.Gov. Ron DeSantis is ordering permitted readers off state highways as Republicans and Democrats call for broader restrictions on technology that police credit with solving crimes and critics warn can track everyday life.WATCH BELOW: Florida puts license plate cameras on the clock amid calls for limitsThe Florida Department of Transportation's Aug. 31 directive revokes approvals issued to local law enforcement agencies for automated license plate readers within state highway rights-of-way. Agencies have 30 days to remove the devices. After that, FDOT says it will remove any covered cameras that remain.The department is also stopping new approvals, citing the rapid growth of the camera networks, reports of misuse and concerns about data privacy.The order covers license plate readers from different manufacturers, including Flock Safety. Its reach is limited, however: Cameras on local roads and private property outside FDOT's jurisdiction are not automatically covered.Automated readers photograph passing vehicles and capture information police can search to locate suspects, stolen cars or missing people. The privacy concern is that the cameras also collect information about motorists who are not suspected of a crime.Florida officers have faced accusations of using those databases to track spouses or former partners, national outlets reported.DeSantis offered a more familiar example Monday: a trip to Buc-ee's."It's really none of the government's damn business if you're doing that, right?" he said.The governor has acknowledged the cameras' usefulness to police while questioning who controls the information and what safeguards prevent abuse. He pointed to New Hampshire as a possible model for restrictions on roadside readers while preserving their use in police vehicles. New Hampshire's law defines a license plate reader as a device mounted to a vehicle and attended and operated by a law enforcement officer.Some law enforcement leaders are defending the technology even as they comply with the state's directive.Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said the county's readers help solve serious crimes but would be taken down following the governor's order, according to Miami Herald reporter Doug Hanks.Flock told Fox Business it supports stronger safeguards while preserving technology it says helps police solve crimes and find missing people.The push for restrictions also extends to the race to succeed DeSantis.Republican nominee Byron Donalds has backed the camera removals and additional reforms. In an interview on Fox Business, he supported the governor's move, according to Florida Politics.Democratic nominee David Jolly has called for a warrant requirement, while saying any new rules must preserve law enforcement's ability to respond to crimes in progress."I would like to see us move to an environment that fully requires a warrant," Jolly said at a news conference last week.Jolly renewed his call for a special session Monday, urging lawmakers to address the issue sooner.Democratic state Rep. Anna Eskamani of Orlando is also pressing for action beyond state highways.In a statement Monday, she supported FDOT's decision but said it leaves cameras operating on city streets, county roads and private properties, including neighborhood entrances and shopping centers.Eskamani urged Central Florida governments to pause new contracts and publish an accounting of existing systems, including how many cameras are deployed, who can search their records, how long information is kept and whether it is shared with agencies outside Florida."Public safety and privacy are not opposing teams," she said.Whether lawmakers act before November's election remains uncertain. DeSantis said Monday he was unsure legislative leaders could reach an agreement that quickly, while leaving open the possibility of action after the election and before he leaves office in January. His full remarks are here.For now, the cameras covered by FDOT's order have a deadline. Lawmakers still have a decision.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents divided over license plate camera removal from state roads
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Transportation's order to remove automated license plate readers from state highways is drawing mixed reactions from Palm Beach County residents.
cards.body:
Reid Mollway, a Palm Beach County resident who supports the removal, said the level of data collection is an invasion of privacy. He said residents are being tracked through data that is not fully clarified and kept for dates that have no expiration.

David Vega, another Palm Beach County resident, said the cameras serve an important public safety purpose and he supports them being there. Vega and others argue the cameras help law enforcement keep communities safer. Another resident said it is something that allows people to walk their street and be on the highways more safely. Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from state highways within 30 days. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police pause license plate readers, limit use to life-threatening situations
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police have announced an operational pause on license plate readers in the city, limiting the technology to circumstances where there is an immediate threat to human life. The city currently has 126 license plate readers throughout Port St. Lucie.

Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the pause is about responding to community concerns. The goal of the pause is to find a path forward that preserves public trust. Niemczyk said the readers are not using biometrics or facial recognition, but instead take pictures of the rear of vehicles. He said the technology is not used for any traffic enforcement, including red light enforcement or speeding enforcement.

Niemczyk said the technology has delivered measurable results, including a 17% reduction in auto burglaries and a reduction in traveling crime. Residents are divided on the technology. Neighbor Joseph Hamm said he thinks the readers are great, while neighbor Peter Schmitt said he thinks they should be illegal, calling them a privacy invasion.

Niemczyk said he wants lawmakers in Tallahassee to get answers from manufacturers like Flock about data retention and work with legislators to provide usage guidelines that protect both the community and officers, and establish consequences for misuse. Niemczyk said the technology has made police more effective, but questioned whether it costs the trust of the community.

You need to respond when the community expresses concern. You need to approach it with an open mind," Niemczyk said.He said the goal of the pause is to find a path forward that preserves public trust."The whole idea of our pause is to figure out how we can re-establish regular use while maintaining the trust of the community," Niemczyk said.Niemczyk also moved to address misconceptions about how the technology works. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Police pause Flock camera use after state revokes permits
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department paused the use of all Automated License Plate Reader technology, known as Flock cameras, after the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for ALPR systems on state roads. The department announced Wednesday that ALPR access will be limited exclusively to exigent circumstances regarding immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm.

Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the department is balancing competing priorities. "On one hand, we have a technology that has proven to be an important tool for our officers and investigators and has helped us protect people and solve crimes," he said. "On the other, we have a responsibility to listen to our community, respect the direction of our state leaders, and ensure our policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety."

The announcement came in response to a memorandum from FDOT regarding the revoking of permits for ALPR systems on state roads. Niemczyk said the department is committed to finding balance and doing what is right for the people it serves.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department will continue to monitor developments at the state level and review any additional guidance as it becomes available.

During the pause, PSLPD says that ALPR access will be limited exclusively to exigent circumstances regarding immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm. cards.headline: Data center proposed for 174 acres off West Midway Road in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center.
cards.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project.

Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. The applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and restaurants or fast food.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. "If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

hero.headline: Tiger Woods scheduled for change-of-plea hearing Wednesday in Martin County DUI case
hero.body:
Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods previously entered a not guilty plea to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. Woods' attorney Douglas Duncan filed a notice Tuesday setting the hearing for 8:30 a.m. Wednesday before Judge Darren Steele at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart. The filing lists the subject of the hearing as a Change of Plea.

The charges stem from a March 27 crash on South Beach Road on Jupiter Island. Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements. They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test.

Legal Analyst Robert Ellis told CBS12 News this change of plea could signal a deal has been reached between prosecutors and the defense. Ellis said prosecutors would consider the fact that Woods sought treatment almost immediately after his arrest, spending six weeks in a rehabilitation program in Switzerland. Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash.

Woods' past could complicate negotiations. In 2017, he resolved a similar case in Palm Beach County through a diversion program that resulted in a reckless driving conviction, meaning that option is no longer available to him. Ellis said prosecutors could still negotiate a plea to reckless driving or another reduced charge, but Woods' prior history may factor into those discussions. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case.

Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements. They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket, according to the arrest affidavit. 'Although they had two pills in his possession, they don't have the clean toxicology evidence that a jury would like to see to prove a DUI," said Ellis. Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test. Whether Woods gets a deal could depend on both his recent actions and his past history. Ellis said prosecutors would consider the fact that Woods sought treatment almost immediately after his arrest, spending six weeks in a rehabilitation program in Switzerland. Ellis expects the defense would use that to argue for leniency. "They'd ask them to credit that, because what we're talking about here are issues of drug and alcohol use, and rehabilitation is an important factor of that," he said. But Woods' past could complicate things. In 2017, he resolved a similar case in Palm Beach County through a diversion program that resulted in a reckless driving conviction, meaning that option is no longer available to him. "He may very well end up in jail," said Ellis. Ellis said prosecutors could still negotiate a plea to reckless driving or another reduced charge, but Woods' prior history may factor into those discussions. "Equal justice under the law means that everyone, Tiger Woods or not, should be treated the same way. It also means that Tiger Woods shouldn't be treated any worse than someone else," he said. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case.

hero.headline: Data center proposed for 174 acres in western St. Lucie County near Interstate 95
hero.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center. The rezoning application stated the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises, but those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project.

Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. The rezoning application requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and restaurants or fast food.

Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area. When asked about the potential data center, she said she hates the idea.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions. Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. If the rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Police pause Flock camera use after state revokes permits on state roads
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Police Department paused the use of all Automated License Plate Reader technology, widely recognized as Flock cameras, after the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for ALPR systems on state roads. The police department announced the operational pause Wednesday following FDOT's memorandum issued Monday.

During the pause, Port St. Lucie police will limit ALPR access exclusively to exigent circumstances involving immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the department faces a balance between using proven crime-solving technology and respecting state leadership and community trust.

The removal order came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control last week. FDOT ordered local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also announced Tuesday it will limit license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons.

Port St. Lucie police said the department will continue to monitor developments at the state level and review any additional guidance as it becomes available. Niemczyk said the department has a responsibility to listen to the community, respect the direction of state leaders, and ensure policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety.

During the pause, PSLPD says that ALPR access will be limited exclusively to exigent circumstances regarding immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk weighed in on the decision to remove pause the use of ALPR technology. See also: Motorcycle crash shuts down I-95 Southbound in Martin County This is a dedicated balance. On one hand, we have a technology that has proven to be an important tool for our officers and investigators and has helped us protect people and solve crimes, he said. On the other, we have a responsibility to listen to our community, respect the direction of our state leaders, and ensure our policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety. We are committed to finding that balance and doing what is right for the people we serve. PSLPD says it will continue to monitor developments at the state level and review any additional guidance as it becomes available.

hero.headline: Indiantown Village Council fires manager, rejects data center pause after resident outcry
hero.body:
The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to terminate Village Manager Taryn Kryzda effective immediately and rejected a proposed temporary pause on new large-scale data center applications after hours of public comment from residents concerned about hyperscale development. The council voted 4-1 against the resolution that would have halted new data center applications while the village drafted regulations addressing infrastructure, utilities and community impacts. Council members said they want new legal counsel to review the proposal and help craft language that can withstand legal scrutiny before bringing it back for consideration.

Shortly after that vote, the council removed Kryzda, who had served as village manager since 2024. The council also voted to remove Village Attorney Wade Vose from the meeting and move forward with obtaining interim legal counsel. Vose had previously submitted his resignation, but council members voted to end his participation in the meeting. Late Tuesday night, the council appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager. Giardino recently served as Stuart's city manager before being fired by the Stuart City Commission last week.

Before the votes, residents spent hours voicing concerns about the potential impact multiple hyperscale data centers could have on the community. Some residents created a website featuring an interactive map highlighting several proposed projects across the area. Penny Kaminsky-Preli used the map to point out developments including Project Growler, a 600,000 square foot hyperscale data center. Resident Eric Miller said he was concerned about the proximity of future projects to schools and parks. "I'm not against them coming to the village. I'm more concerned with their proximity to things like the school or field elementary school. I'm more concerned with the proximity to Booker Park," Miller said.

Former Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback urged council members to use authority recently granted to local governments by state lawmakers. "There have been 19 moratoriums that have been passed in Florida this year. Not a single one of them have been challenged by a data center plaintiff," Fishback said. Village leaders told CBS12 News they expect to have interim legal counsel in place soon and hope to bring a revised data center resolution back before the council within the next week or two. As she left Village Hall, Kryzda told CBS12 News, "I'm happy to go home early."
hero.article_text: A packed crowd filled Village Hall Tuesday night as residents urged leaders to hit the pause button on future hyperscale data center projects . But by the end of the meeting, the debate over data centers had led to a major shakeup in village leadership. After hours of public comment, the Indiantown Village Council voted 4-1 against a proposed resolution that would have temporarily paused new large-scale data center applications while the village drafted regulations addressing infrastructure, utilities and community impacts. Council members said they want new legal counsel to review the proposal and help craft language that can withstand legal scrutiny before bringing it back for consideration. Shortly after that vote, the council voted to terminate Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had served the village since 2024, effective immediately. The council also voted to remove Village Attorney Wade Vose from the meeting and move forward with obtaining interim legal counsel. Vose had previously submitted his resignation, but council members voted to end his participation in the meeting and proceed in a different direction. Late Tuesday night, the council appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager. Giardino recently served as Stuart's city manager before being fired by the Stuart City Commission last week. Council members said the leadership changes reflect a desire to move the village in a new direction as it tackles major issues, including future data center development. As she left Village Hall, Kryzda offered a brief response to CBS12 News. "I'm happy to go home early." Before the vote, residents spent hours voicing concerns about the potential impact multiple hyperscale data centers could have on the community. Some residents created a website featuring an interactive map highlighting several proposed projects across the area. Penny Kaminsky-Preli used the map to point out some of those developments. "This is Project Growler, another 600,000 hyperscale data center. Another one in the application." Others worried about how close future projects could be to schools, parks and neighborhoods. "I'm not against them coming to the village. I'm more concerned with their proximity to things like the school or field elementary school. I'm more concerned with the proximity to Booker Park," resident Eric Miller said. Former Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback urged council members to use what he described as authority recently granted to local governments by state lawmakers. "There have been 19 moratoriums that have been passed in Florida this year. Not a single one of them have been challenged by a data center plaintiff," Fishback said. Village leaders told CBS12 News they expect to have interim legal counsel in place soon and hope to bring a revised data center resolution back before the council within the next week or two.

hero.headline: Martin County Sheriff warns residents less safe after state orders license plate reader removal
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation ordered local agencies on Monday to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, prompting Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek to warn Tuesday that the decision makes county residents fundamentally less safe. The memorandum came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control last week.

Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with help from the cameras, including the arrest of former President Donald Trump's would-be assassin, the rescue of two young girls headed to Nebraska with a kidnapper last year, and the arrest of a traveling rooftop burglary crew. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised license plate readers like Flock cameras after they aided in a homicide arrest last month. Flowers said a murderer was caught and taken off the streets because of the Flock system.

Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will limit license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder called for meaningful legislation that regulates camera use and protects privacy while allowing the community to keep the cameras and remain safe.

Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record. He said he would support a public professional auditing system if people still do not trust law enforcement. Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras because he considers them an invasion of privacy. Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe, while neighbor Kristina Ramsey said the cameras have helped catch a lot of criminals.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Police pause Flock camera use after state revokes road permits
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department announced an operational pause on all Automated License Plate Reader technology, widely recognized as Flock cameras, following a Florida Department of Transportation memorandum revoking permits for ALPR systems on state roads. The pause took effect Wednesday.

During the pause, PSLPD says ALPR access will be limited exclusively to exigent circumstances regarding immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm.

Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the decision reflects a balance between technology that has proven an important tool for officers and investigators and the responsibility to listen to the community and respect state direction. He said the department has a responsibility to ensure its policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety.

PSLPD says it will continue to monitor developments at the state level and review any additional guidance as it becomes available. The cameras have helped the department protect people and solve crimes, according to the chief.

cards.headline: Data center proposed for 174 acres in western St. Lucie County near Interstate 95
cards.teaser: Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center.
cards.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use to allow for a data center. The rezoning application said the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises.

Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. The applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and restaurants or fast food.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area and opposes the idea. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

cards.headline: Body found in Hutchinson Island mangroves believed to be missing Oklahoma visitor
cards.teaser: A body discovered in mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen at Chastain Beach on Aug. 26.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is investigating a body found in the mangroves just north of the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island that is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen at Chastain Beach on Aug. 26. Investigators are waiting for a positive identification, but Sheriff John Budensiek said he believes the body belongs to Debevec because the clothing matches what Debevec was last seen wearing in surveillance video.

Debevec's family filed a missing person report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge. Deputies later discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach. The Sheriff's Office then searched the area of Hutchinson Island by land, sea and air.

The search continued through Tuesday morning when deputies found Debevec's backpack hanging high in a tree. As they continued through the thick mangroves and brushed sea grapes, they located the deceased body. The body was found heavily decomposed.

The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death, looking for signs of trauma and performing a toxicology report. Debevec's family says he has gone missing before and has a history of substance abuse, but says he had gotten clean.

hero.headline: Speeding driver crashes into two parked trucks on SW Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
A speeding driver crashed into two parked trucks on Southwest Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie around 3:40 p.m., causing extensive damage and renewing resident concerns about chronic speeding on the residential road. Security video recorded the crash, which shows a black truck traveling at a high rate of speed before going off the road into the grass and slamming into the two parked trucks.

The driver of the black truck sustained only minor injuries, Port St. Lucie police said. The two parked trucks, both owned by Rocky Burkhead and essential to his pressure washing business, sustained extensive damage. Burkhead said he had to rent a U-Haul to continue working.

Neighbors said the crash highlights a persistent speeding problem on Southwest Lucero Drive, where the speed limit is 25 mph but drivers rarely adhere to it. Courtney Gray said people fly by on the road all the time. The lack of sidewalks compounds the danger for residents who walk along the road with children and pets. Gray said she walks every day with her baby in a stroller and was thankful she was not home when the crash happened.

Burkhead suggested Port St. Lucie police station officers in the area and issue heavy fines to address the speeding. Gray said speed bumps may be needed to prevent similar crashes. Port St. Lucie police have not responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols.
hero.article_text: Two parked trucks were heavily damaged in a violent crash in Port St. Security video recorded the crash, which shows a black truck traveling at a high rate of speed on SW Lucero Drive around 3:40 p.m. The truck goes off the road into the grass and then slams into the two parked trucks. "When I heard the crash, I thought it was thunder," Elaine Harmon, a neighbor, said. "I heard a loud explosion," said another neighbor, Rocky Burkhead. "Thought it was just lightning like we've been having over the last few days." But when Burkhead stepped outside, he realized the situation was far worse than a weather-related incident. "I had no idea what to think. I was just at a loss for words. My first concern was, 'Is he OK?'" Burkhead said. Lucie police said the man in the black truck sustained only minor injuries. However, Burkhead said the damage to the two parked trucks hit in the collision was extensive. Both trucks belong to Burkhead and are essential for his pressure washing business. I had to rent a U-Haul today. You're limited on what you can do, how far you can go," Burkhead said. Neighbors said the crash is the most dramatic example of speeding on Southwest Lucero Drive but emphasized it is not an isolated incident. The speed limit on the road is 25 mph, but residents said drivers rarely adhere to it. "People do fly by on this road all the time," Courtney Gray, a neighbor, said. "There's a big problem with speeding on this road," Burkhead said. Residents are particularly concerned because the road lacks sidewalks, yet many people walk along it with children and pets. "I walk every day with (my baby) in the stroller or whatever. I'm just so thankful we weren't home when it happened," Gray said. "I think what they need to do is put some officers in the area, pull a few people over with some heavy-duty fines," Burkhead said. "Seems like something like this is going to keep happening if we don't have speed bumps," Gray said. Lucie police have not yet responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols. cards.headline: Two people, dog escape Jensen Beach garage fire caused by charging lithium-ion battery
cards.teaser: Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after a charging lithium-ion battery burst into flames.
cards.body:
Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after firefighters quickly contained the blaze, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The fire was reported just after 6:30 a.m. in the 2700 block of Northeast Cypress Lane. When crews arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage of the home.

According to the homeowner, a lithium-ion battery had been charging in the garage before the fire started. Firefighters immediately evacuated the residence and worked to contain the flames, preventing the fire from spreading beyond the garage. Officials said crews successfully extinguished the fire, and no neighboring structures were threatened.

Fire rescue officials called the incident a close call and are reminding residents to follow proper lithium-ion battery safety practices. They encourage people to unplug batteries once they are fully charged to help prevent overheating and potential fires. For additional information on lithium-ion battery safety, residents can visit the National Fire Protection Association's website.

cards.headline: Body found in Hutchinson Island mangroves believed to be missing Oklahoma visitor
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is investigating a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island. Investigators believe the body belongs to Michael Anthony Debevec II, who was reported missing after visiting Chastain Beach.
cards.body:
A body discovered in the mangroves on Hutchinson Island is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen on August 26 at Chastain Beach, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The body was found just north of the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island on Tuesday.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the clothing on the heavily decomposed body matched what Debevec was last seen wearing in surveillance video. Debevec's family filed a missing person's report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge. Deputies later discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office searched the area by land, sea and air. Deputies found Debevec's backpack hanging high in a tree south of the House of Refuge before locating the deceased body in thick mangroves and sea grapes. The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death and performing a toxicology report. Debevec's family said he had a history of substance abuse but had gotten clean.

hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office recovered a body Tuesday from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge following an extensive search for a missing Port St. Lucie man. Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed the identity, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Michael Anthony Debevec was believed to have been wearing. Budensiek said a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, which led the family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. on August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. The discovery of the wallet and vehicle prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. Budensiek said there was a lot of decomposition, making it impossible to determine cause of death.

Debevec's family was notified that a body was found. Budensiek said investigators believe they found Debevec but could not confirm whether it was him.

hero.headline: Florida orders removal of automated license plate readers from state highways within 30 days
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from state highways within 30 days. The department cited concerns over rapid expansion, data privacy, misuse and surveillance schemes in announcing the directive.

The announcement follows public statements by Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the technology out of control days earlier and raised concerns about Florida becoming a surveillance state. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records. The decision affects cameras operated by local law enforcement agencies and municipalities that have installed the devices on state-controlled roadways.

Palm Beach County residents expressed divided opinions on the order. Reid Mollway said the level of data collection represents an invasion of privacy, noting that tracking data is not fully clarified and is kept for dates that have no expiration. David Vega and other residents defended the cameras as serving an important public safety purpose. Vega said the cameras allow people to walk streets and use highways more safely.

Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. Multiple local law enforcement agencies have been contacted for comment but have not yet responded to the state order.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office to host 9/11 memorial ceremony at fairgrounds
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office will host a communitywide memorial ceremony Friday at the Indian River County Fairgrounds & Expo Center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office will host a communitywide memorial ceremony Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, at the Indian River County Fairgrounds & Expo Center at 7955 58th Ave. in Vero Beach. The ceremony will honor the nearly 3,000 victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and recognize the courage and sacrifice of first responders who responded to the tragedy.

Residents, veterans, students, families and community organizations are encouraged to attend and stand together in remembrance, honor and unity. The event marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.

The ceremony is part of a series of remembrance events planned across Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties to mark the milestone anniversary of the terrorist attacks that changed America.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners receive notice about Waste Pro settlement credits on property tax bills
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with Waste Pro will appear on their property tax bills.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are receiving notices in the mail explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with Waste Pro will show up on their property tax bills. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro, the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit.

The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. Council members agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.
cards.article_text: Lucie homeowners are finding a flyer in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro , the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. According to the city's proposal, about 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit. One resident recounted her first reaction to getting the letter. I thought it was going to be money, not on my taxes, said Deborah Koon-Martin, a PSL homeowner. That difference is the part homeowners are most likely to notice when the notice arrives. Not every property qualifies for the larger amount. The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. You can use the money for other things. You're going to pay your taxes anyway, so it's not really helping, Koon-Martin said. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience. See also: West Palm Beach man arrested with gun at private school, police say When Koon-Martin was asked what she wanted from the city, her answer was clear. Because it makes it better. You have maggots crawling out of the trash. I’d rather go back to twice a week, said Koon-Martin. Council members also agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. "It's the taxpayers' money. The taxpayers were the ones who were wronged," Councilman Anthony Bonna said. The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Lucie's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Residents have continued pressing the city over once-a-week pickup, and the council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

cards.headline: Speeding driver crashes into two parked trucks on SW Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A violent crash on Southwest Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie damaged two parked trucks and highlighted ongoing speeding concerns on the residential road.
cards.body:
Two parked trucks were heavily damaged in a crash on Southwest Lucero Drive in Port St. Lucie. Security video recorded the crash, which shows a black truck traveling at a high rate of speed on SW Lucero Drive around 3:40 p.m. The truck goes off the road into the grass and then slams into the two parked trucks. Port St. Lucie police said the man in the black truck sustained only minor injuries.

The two parked trucks hit in the collision belong to Rocky Burkhead and are essential for his pressure washing business. Burkhead said he had to rent a U-Haul and is limited on what he can do and how far he can go. Neighbors said the crash is the most dramatic example of speeding on Southwest Lucero Drive but emphasized it is not an isolated incident. The speed limit on the road is 25 mph, but residents said drivers rarely adhere to it.

Residents are particularly concerned because the road lacks sidewalks, yet many people walk along it with children and pets. Courtney Gray said she walks every day with her baby in the stroller. Burkhead said officers should pull people over with heavy-duty fines. Gray said speed bumps are needed to prevent similar crashes. Port St. Lucie police have not yet responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols.

"When I heard the crash, I thought it was thunder," Elaine Harmon, a neighbor, said. "I heard a loud explosion," said another neighbor, Rocky Burkhead. "Thought it was just lightning like we've been having over the last few days." But when Burkhead stepped outside, he realized the situation was far worse than a weather-related incident. "I had no idea what to think. I was just at a loss for words. My first concern was, 'Is he OK?'" Burkhead said. Lucie police said the man in the black truck sustained only minor injuries. However, Burkhead said the damage to the two parked trucks hit in the collision was extensive. Both trucks belong to Burkhead and are essential for his pressure washing business. I had to rent a U-Haul today. You're limited on what you can do, how far you can go," Burkhead said. Neighbors said the crash is the most dramatic example of speeding on Southwest Lucero Drive but emphasized it is not an isolated incident. The speed limit on the road is 25 mph, but residents said drivers rarely adhere to it. "People do fly by on this road all the time," Courtney Gray, a neighbor, said. "There's a big problem with speeding on this road," Burkhead said. Residents are particularly concerned because the road lacks sidewalks, yet many people walk along it with children and pets. "I walk every day with (my baby) in the stroller or whatever. I'm just so thankful we weren't home when it happened," Gray said. "I think what they need to do is put some officers in the area, pull a few people over with some heavy-duty fines," Burkhead said. "Seems like something like this is going to keep happening if we don't have speed bumps," Gray said. Lucie police have not yet responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols. hero.headline: Tiger Woods scheduled for change-of-plea hearing Wednesday in Martin County DUI case
hero.body:
Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods' attorney, Douglas Duncan, filed a notice Tuesday setting the hearing for 8:30 a.m. Wednesday before Judge Darren Steele at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart. The filing lists the subject of the hearing as a Change of Plea.

The development marks a change from Woods' previous position in the case. In March, the 50-year-old golf legend entered a not guilty plea to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. Court records do not indicate what plea Woods intends to enter Wednesday or whether the hearing is part of a negotiated plea agreement.

The charges stem from a March 27 crash on South Beach Road on Jupiter Island. Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements. They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket, according to the arrest affidavit.

Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case. Woods was booked into the Martin County Jail and released later that night after posting $1,150 bail.

hero.headline: Florida orders removal of license plate cameras from state roads within 30 days
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, citing concerns over rapid expansion, data privacy, misuse and surveillance schemes. The directive includes Flock cameras and comes days after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control and raised concerns about Florida becoming a surveillance state. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records.

The decision is drawing mixed reactions from residents. Reid Mollway, a Palm Beach County resident, supports the move. The level of data collection I feel is an invasion of privacy, Mollway said. We're being tracked through data that is not fully clarified and kept for dates that have no expiration. David Vega, another Palm Beach County resident, said the cameras serve an important public safety purpose. I support them being there, Vega said. Vega and others argue the cameras help law enforcement keep communities safer.

The crackdown is also drawing political criticism. Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. Local law enforcement agencies have been contacted for comment on how the removal order will affect their operations. Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw responded but did not provide details in the statement.

The 30-day removal deadline means local agencies must dismantle the camera systems from state roads by early October. The order affects cameras installed along highways throughout Florida and represents a significant shift in state policy on automated surveillance technology on public roads.

cards.headline: DeSantis and Byron Donalds to share Tampa stage as Florida Republicans seek unity after primary
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis and Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds are scheduled to appear together at a Republican leadership forum in Tampa on Tuesday, marking an apparent thaw after a contentious primary.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis and Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds are scheduled to share a stage Tuesday at a Republican leadership forum in Tampa. Attorney General James Uthmeier, Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson are also expected at the event. The appearance follows a primary campaign that exposed a persistent gap between Donalds and the outgoing governor.

DeSantis declined to endorse anyone in the Republican primary, including Lt. Jay Collins, the lieutenant governor he appointed in 2025. DeSantis previously said Donalds had not been part of his administration's victories in Florida. Donalds suggested the friction stemmed from his decision to endorse Donald Trump over DeSantis during the 2024 presidential primary. Donalds won nearly 48 percent of the vote in an 11-candidate field, finishing well ahead of Collins, who took roughly 25 percent.

Tonight, the primary is over, Donalds told supporters on primary night. Tonight, we put aside our differences. Tonight, we are one united Republican Party. Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia predicted the GOP would move past the primary and unite around its statewide slate. I think we're having a Kumbaya moment, Ingoglia said in August. We're all going to get in the same boat, rowing in the same direction. The general election is in November, and Donalds will face Democratic nominee David Jolly in the race to succeed the term-limited DeSantis.
